  • Expand rough notes into a finished document.
  • Simplify the language.
  • Check grammar, punctuation and style.
  • Extract the key points.
  • Rewrite in plain language for accessibility purposes.
  • Rewrite in a friendly and encouraging tone.
  • Break down the content into simple step-by-step instructions.
  • Generate frequently asked questions.
  • Rewrite for beginners.
  • Convert into a summary email.
  • Extract action items.
  • Paraphrase.
  • Rewrite as a short social media post.
  • Summarise as a meeting summary.
  • Rewrite as a speech draft.

Leasey Word creates a document backup before applying replacement text.

You can also press Control+Z to undo the change.

Please refer to the later section of this chapter to see how automatic replacement of text is controlled.

Choosing the right tool.

Use Ask a question about the text when you want an answer, not a rewrite.

Example:

You have selected a paragraph from a letter and want to know what it is asking you to do.

Use Dictionary when you want to understand a word.

Example:

You are reading a document and do not know what a word means.

Use Thesaurus when you want a different word.

Example:

You have used the word important too many times and want another suitable word.

Use Summarise when the text is too long and you want the main idea.

Example:

You have copied a long email into Leasey Word and want the main points.

Use Formal rewrite when the text needs to sound professional.

Example:

You have written a complaint or business email.

Use Expand rough notes when you have ideas but not a finished document.

Example:

You have typed bullet points for an announcement and want a complete message.

Use Simplify when the text is too complicated.

Example:

You have a technical paragraph and want it to be easier to read.

Use Grammar, punctuation and style check when the text is finished but needs polishing.

Example:

You have written an email and want to check it before sending.

Use Extract key points when you want the important items as a list.

Example:

You have a long document and want the main facts.

Use Plain language for accessibility when the text needs to be especially clear.

Example:

You are writing instructions for a wide range of users.

Use Friendly rewrite when the text sounds too cold.

Example:

You are writing a welcome message or support response.

Use Step-by-step instructions when the text describes a process.

Example:

You have a paragraph explaining how to do something and want it turned into steps.

Use FAQs when you want likely questions and answers.

Example:

You have written a help topic and want a short FAQ section.

Use Beginner rewrite when the reader may not understand the subject yet.

Example:

You are writing a first-time guide.

Use Summary email when you want notes turned into an email.

Example:

You have meeting notes and want to send someone a short summary.

Use Action items when you want a to-do list.

Example:

You have meeting notes and want to know what needs to be done.

Use Paraphrase when you want the same meaning in different words.

Example:

A sentence is awkward but the meaning is correct.

Use Social media post when you want a very short announcement.

Example:

You want a brief post for Mastodon, X or another service.

Use Meeting summary when the text contains meeting notes.

Example:

You have rough notes from a meeting and want a cleaner summary.

Use Constructive feedback when you want advice but do not want the document changed.

Example:

You want to know whether your article is clear and whether anything is missing.

Use Speech draft when the text will be spoken aloud.

Example:

You are preparing a short talk, presentation or radio script.

Size safeguards.

The same size safeguard applies to selected text and whole documents.

If the text is too large to send to ChatGPT in one request, Leasey Word displays a clear message and does not send it.

As a simple guide, use ChatGPT Text Tools with documents or selections of about 40 pages or less.

What the Options check boxes change.

There are two Options check boxes which affect ChatGPT replacement tools.

Open Options with Control+Comma.

The two check boxes are:

  • Review individual ChatGPT changes before applying.
  • Preview full ChatGPT result before applying.

They sound similar, but they do different jobs.

Review individual ChatGPT changes before applying.

This option is useful when you want to inspect individual changes.

For example, if you ask ChatGPT to check spelling or grammar, you may want to see that it has changed:

Goood

to:

Good

The Review ChatGPT Changes dialog tries to identify words or phrases which ChatGPT appears to have changed.

You can accept or reject individual changes before applying the result.

This is particularly useful when the text contains:

  • Names of people.
  • Product names.
  • Place names.
  • Unusual spellings.
  • Technical terms.
  • Words which ChatGPT may misunderstand.

For example, suppose your document contains the name:

Neil

ChatGPT may suggest:

Neal

If Neal is correct, accept the change.

If the spelling should be Niall, Tab to the Replacement Edit Field, change the replacement to Niall, then accept it.

The Review ChatGPT Changes dialog contains:

  • Changes List Box.
  • Context Edit Field.
  • Original Edit Field.
  • Replacement Edit Field.
  • Accept Button.
  • Reject Button.
  • Apply Button.
  • Cancel Button.

When the dialog opens, focus is in the Changes List Box.

Each item describes one proposed change.

Press Up Arrow and Down Arrow to move through the list.

The Context Edit Field is read-only. It shows the original sentence and the replacement sentence.

The Original Edit Field is read-only. It shows the original text for the selected change.

The Replacement Edit Field can be edited. It shows the text ChatGPT proposes to use.

To accept or reject individual changes:

Step 1. Move to a change in the Changes List Box.

Step 2. If you want to check the sentence, press Tab to move to the Context Edit Field and review it with the Arrow keys.

Step 3. Press Tab to move to the Original Edit Field if you want to review the exact original text.

Step 4. Press Tab to move to the Replacement Edit Field.

Step 5. If the replacement is correct, leave it as it is. If it is wrong, edit the replacement text.

Step 6. Press Tab to move to Accept or Reject.

Step 7. Press Enter or Space.

If you accept a change, it is marked as accepted.

If you reject a change, it is marked as rejected.

When you have finished, Tab to Apply and press Enter or Space.

Leasey Word applies the accepted changes and keeps your original text for rejected changes.

If you want to accept all changes without reviewing them one by one, press Enter while focused in the Changes List Box.

Press Escape or activate Cancel to leave the document unchanged.

Preview full ChatGPT result before applying.

This option is useful when you want to see the whole ChatGPT result before it changes your document.

For example, suppose you choose:

Summarise the main points concisely in plain UK English.

If Preview full ChatGPT result before applying is checked, Leasey Word shows the summary before placing it in the document.

You can then decide what to do.

Press Escape if you do not want to use the result.

Or review and edit the replacement text.

Then Tab to Accept and press Enter or Space if you want to apply it.

This is useful for tools such as:

  • Summary.
  • Formal rewrite.
  • Friendly rewrite.
  • Plain language rewrite.
  • Step-by-step instructions.
  • Summary email.
  • Social media post.
  • Speech draft.
The easiest way to think about the two options.

Review individual ChatGPT changes before applying lets you inspect individual changes.

Preview full ChatGPT result before applying lets you inspect the whole result.

You can use either option, both options, or neither option.

If you are unsure, leave both options checked until you are comfortable with how ChatGPT Text Tools behave.

Translate Text.

Translate Text uses ChatGPT to translate text directly inside Leasey Word.

If text is selected, only the selected text is translated.

If no text is selected, the whole document is translated.

To translate text:

Step 1. Select the text you want to translate, or leave nothing selected if you want to translate the whole document.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+E.

The Translate Text dialog opens.

Step 3. Focus is in the Translate to Combo Box.

Choose a language such as English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Polish, Ukrainian, Welsh, Irish, Japanese or Chinese.

You can also type another language if it is not in the list.

Step 4. Press Tab to move to the Text Edit Field if you want to review or amend the text before it is sent.

Step 5. Press Tab to move to OK and press Enter or Space.

ChatGPT detects the source language automatically.

When the translation is complete, the translated text replaces the selected text. If no text was selected, it replaces the source document text.

Translate Text uses the same Leasey/OpenAI API key as the other ChatGPT features.

Recovering Bookmarks After Moving a Document.

If you moved a document to a different folder, Leasey Word may treat it as a different document because bookmarks are stored against the document path.

To recover those bookmarks:

Step 1. Open the moved document in Leasey Word.

Step 2. Open the File menu with Alt+F and choose Recover Bookmarks from Previous Location by pressing the Down Arrow key until the item is reached, then press Enter.

Step 3. The dialog shows the current document path.

In the Previous folder Edit Field, type or browse to the folder where the document used to be stored.

An Edit Field is available into which you can type the path. Pressing Tab allows you to reach a Browse Button to browse to the folder using standard Windows techniques.

Step 4. Press Enter when the folder is located.

Leasey Word combines that previous folder with the current file name and transfers any bookmarks, Leasey Points, saved cursor position, recent file entry and document backups to the current document location.

JAWS should announce:

Bookmarks recovered

Document Composition Indentation.

It is possible to increase or decrease paragraph text by a specific amount.

Indentation is useful when you want part of a document to stand out from the surrounding text.

For example, you might indent a quotation, a set of instructions, a note within a larger document, or a paragraph which belongs under a heading.

It can also be helpful when writing structured material where some paragraphs are subordinate to others.

This is document formatting, not spaces or tabs typed into the document.

  • Each indentation level moves the paragraph approximately half an inch to the right.
  • Press Control+Alt+Right Arrow to increase indentation.
  • Press Control+Alt+Left Arrow to decrease indentation.

The command applies to selected text if text is selected.

Otherwise, it applies to the current line.

JAWS should announce:

Indent level followed by the level number.

For example:

Indent level 2

In Options, activated with Control+Comma, there is a checkbox entitled Speak document composition indentation level when moving by line.

When this is checked, Leasey Word announces the document composition indentation level when you move to a line with a different indentation level.

Code Indentation.

If you are writing code, HTML, JSON, JAWS scripts, PHP, configuration files, or similar text, indentation is usually made with actual spaces or tab characters.

This is different from document composition indentation.

In Options, there is a checkbox entitled Speak code indentation when moving by line.

When this is checked, Leasey Word announces the actual leading spaces and tabs at the start of a line as you move with Up Arrow and Down Arrow.

For example, JAWS may announce:

No code indentation

Or:

4 spaces

Or:

1 tab, 2 spaces

This can help you check whether code lines are aligned correctly.

Inserting a LeaseyNote into a Document.

If you are a heavy user of Leasey Notes, you may wish to bring one of them into your document.

Step 1. Press Control+Shift+L.

Step 2. A list of Leasey Notes is shown.

Step 3. Press the Down Arrow key to choose a note.

Step 4. Press Enter to insert the selected note text into the current document at the cursor position.

If text is selected in the document, the selected text is replaced.

JAWS should announce:

Inserted LeaseyNote followed by the note title.

Page Movement.

For documents which contain real page markers, such as locally extracted PDF files, Leasey Word can report the current page.

Press Page Up or Page Down.

Leasey Word moves to the previous or next page marker.

JAWS should announce:

Page followed by the page number.

For example:

Page 4

If the document does not contain real page markers, Page Up and Page Down perform normal Edit Field movement.

Go To Page.

To move to a specific page if the document contains page markers:

Step 1. Press Control+G.

Step 2. Type the page number and press Enter.

Step 3. Leasey Word moves to that page if the current document contains page markers.

This is most useful for PDF documents which have been extracted into page order.

JAWS should announce:

Page followed by the page number.

Sending Text to LeaseySocial.

If you use LeaseySocial, Leasey Word can send the current document or selected text directly to the LeaseySocial compose window.

This is useful if you draft social media posts in Leasey Word because you can use the word processor features first, then move the finished text into LeaseySocial without copying and pasting manually.

To send text to LeaseySocial:

Step 1. Write or open the text you want to post.

Step 2. If you only want to send part of the document, select that text.

If no text is selected, Leasey Word sends the whole document.

Step 3. Press Control+Alt+S.

LeaseySocial opens.

If more than one account is available, LeaseySocial asks which account you want to use.

Step 4. Choose the account if asked with the Up and Down Arrow keys. Then press Enter.

Step 5. The normal LeaseySocial New Post dialog opens with the text already inserted.

Step 6. Review or edit the post as usual.

Step 7. Send the post from LeaseySocial when you are ready by pressing Enter.

Leasey Word does not post automatically.

It only prepares the text and opens LeaseySocial so you remain in control of the final post.

The Context Menu.

This is a menu of actions which are relevant to the text or word you are focused upon.

The Context Menu is especially useful if you do not remember the shortcut for a command.

It is also useful because it confirms what actions are available in the current situation.

To open the Context Menu:

Step 1. Move to the document Edit Field.

Step 2. Press the Applications Key. On many keyboards, this key is near the right Control key.

Step 3. If your keyboard does not have an Applications Key, press Shift+F10.

Step 4. Use Up Arrow and Down Arrow to move through the menu.

Step 5. Press Enter on the command you want.

In normal editing, the Context Menu is the standard Edit Field menu provided by Windows.

It may contain commands such as:

  • Undo.
  • Cut.
  • Copy.
  • Paste.
  • Delete.
  • Select All.

For example, suppose you want to copy a paragraph but cannot remember the copy shortcut.

Step 1. Select the paragraph.

Step 2. Press the Applications Key or Shift+F10.

Step 3. Press Down Arrow until you hear Copy.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Step 5. The selected text is copied to the Windows Clipboard.

The Context Menu is also useful with Quick Navigation spelling errors.

If Quick Navigation Mode is on and you have moved to a misspelled word with M or Shift+M, press the Applications Key or Shift+F10.

Leasey Word opens a spelling menu containing suggestions for the misspelled word.

It also contains:

  • Ignore.
  • Ignore All.
  • Add to Dictionary.

For example, suppose Quick Navigation finds a misspelled word and you want to choose a correction.

Step 1. Press Insert+Z to turn Quick Navigation Mode on.

Step 2. Press M to move to the next misspelling.

Step 3. Press the Applications Key or Shift+F10.

Step 4. Move through the suggestions with Up Arrow and Down Arrow.

Step 5. Press Enter on the suggestion you want.

Leasey Word changes the word and announces what it changed the word to.

The Context Menu is not intended to replace shortcut keys.

Instead, it gives you a convenient way to discover and use commands while you are learning the application.

Document and Writing Tools.

Leasey Word can be used as a general word processor, but it can also help you write documents which are intended for web pages, documentation systems, blog posts, podcast show notes, help files and other structured text.

This is where Document and Writing Tools become useful.

These tools help you create HTML and Markdown without needing to remember every character of the syntax. This matters because both HTML and Markdown are precise. A missing bracket, slash, quotation mark or blank line can mean that a heading is not recognised, a list does not form correctly, a link does not work, or a table is not rendered as expected.

If you are working in Leasey Word, this is now the preferred way of creating HTML and Markdown components. The separate HTML Assistant and Markdown chapters remain useful because those tools can still be used in other text editing environments. However, when your document is already open in Leasey Word, Document and Writing Tools give you a more integrated approach.

You can use the tools in two ways.

You can place the cursor where the new component should be inserted, then let Leasey Word ask for the information it needs.

You can also select text which already exists, then use the tool to wrap that selected text in the appropriate HTML or Markdown. With the exception of creating tables, this is by far the preferred method as you have maximum control.

For example, you can select a line of text and turn it into a heading, select several lines and turn them into a list, or select text and turn it into a link.

Opening Document and Writing Tools.

Step 1. Open or create a document in Leasey Word.

Step 2. Move to the place where the HTML or Markdown should be inserted.

Step 3. If you want the command to work on existing text, select that text first.

Step 4. Press Control+Shift+H.

You can also press Alt+Control+Windows+H.

The Document and Writing Tools dialog opens.

The dialog contains:

  • Format Combo Box.
  • Component List.
  • Insert Button.
  • Cancel Button.

The Format Combo Box contains:

  • HTML.
  • Markdown.

Choose HTML if you are writing HTML source code or a document which will be published directly as a web page.

Choose Markdown if you are writing a Markdown document, or if you want to create structured plain text which can later be converted to HTML or Word.

After choosing the format, Tab to the Component List. Use Up Arrow and Down Arrow to choose the component you want, then press Enter.

Leasey Word remembers the last format and component you used.

For example, if you last inserted an HTML Link, the next time the dialog opens HTML is selected and Link is highlighted in the Component List.

Focus still starts on the Format Combo Box so the dialog is predictable and matches the normal Tab order.

Leasey Word asks any further questions if responses are needed. For example, a link asks for a web address. An image asks for the image source and alternative text. A table asks for column headings and row information.

When the information has been entered, Leasey Word inserts the appropriate HTML or Markdown at the cursor position, or wraps the selected text where appropriate.

JAWS should announce the format and component inserted.

For example:

HTML Link inserted

or:

Markdown Heading 2 inserted

You can press Insert+F1 in the dialog if you need additional guidance.

Why HTML and Markdown Matter.

HTML is the language used to structure web pages. It allows you to identify headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, tables and other parts of a page.

A well-structured HTML page is not only better visually. It is usually easier for a screen-reader user to navigate because headings, links, lists and tables can be identified properly.

Markdown is a lighter form of markup. It is written as plain text and is widely used for documentation, notes, web publishing, show notes, technical instructions and many other kinds of writing.

Markdown is often easier to read while you are writing. For example, a Markdown heading may begin with one or more number or hash signs. A Markdown link can be written as visible text followed by a web address in brackets. A Markdown table can be created with plain text rows and separator lines.

The advantage is that Markdown stays readable as text. The disadvantage is that the syntax still needs to be accurate if you want a good result when it is converted to HTML or Word.

Leasey Word helps with both approaches.

HTML Components.

When the Format Combo Box is set to HTML, the Component List can include items such as:

  • Heading 1 through to Heading 6.
  • Paragraph.
  • Line break.
  • Link.
  • Email link.
  • Numbered list.
  • Bulleted list.
  • Block quote.
  • Table.
  • Image.
  • CSS style block.
  • Horizontal rule.
  • Full HTML document.
  • Build Table of Contents.

Leasey Word creates the correct HTML markup for you.

HTML Headings.

HTML headings are used to organise a page into sections.

Heading 1 is normally used for the main title of the page. Heading 2 is used for major sections. Heading 3 and below are used for sub-sections.

Step 1. Move to the place where the heading should be inserted, or select the existing heading text.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose the heading level you want.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. If Leasey Word asks for the heading text, type it and press Enter.

If text was selected first, Leasey Word should use the selected text as the heading text.

HTML Paragraphs and Line Breaks.

A paragraph is a block of text. In HTML, paragraphs should be marked properly so browsers and screen readers can identify them as separate units.

Step 1. Move to the place where the paragraph should be inserted, or select existing paragraph text.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Paragraph.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. Type the paragraph text if requested. Press Enter to create line breaks.

Step 7. Press Tab to reach the OK Button and press Enter or Space.

HTML Links.

A link consists of two parts: the destination and the visible text.

The destination is the web address, such as:

hartgenconsultancy.com

The visible text is what the reader hears or sees, such as:

Visit Hartgen Consultancy

Step 1. Type or select the visible link text.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Link.

Step 5. When asked for the web address, type or paste it and press Enter.

Step 6. If asked for the visible link text, type it and press Enter.

Leasey Word creates the HTML link.

If the web address is long, it is often easier to copy it to the Windows Clipboard before opening Document and Writing Tools. You can then paste it into the web address field with Control+V.

HTML Email Links.

An email link opens a new email message addressed to the email address you specify.

Step 1. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 2. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 3. Press Tab and choose Email Link.

Step 4. Type the email address, such as support@hartgenconsultancy.com, and press Enter.

Step 5. Type the visible link text, such as Email technical support, and press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts the email link.

HTML Lists.

HTML supports numbered lists and bulleted lists.

Use a numbered list when the order matters. Step-by-step instructions are a good example.

Use a bulleted list when the order does not matter. A list of features or choices is a good example.

To create a new HTML list while writing:

Step 1. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 2. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 3. Press Tab and choose Numbered List or Bulleted List.

Step 4. Type each item to be included in the list on a separate line. For example:

  • John.
  • Mary.
  • Jane.

Step 5. When you want to end the list, press Tab to reach the OK Button and press Enter or Space.

To convert existing lines into a list:

Step 1. Select the lines for the list.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Numbered List or Bulleted List.

Step 5. Press Enter.

HTML Tables.

A table presents information in rows and columns.

Tables should be used for genuine tabular information, not merely to position text visually.

Before creating a table, think about the column headings. For example, if you are creating a table of people and scores, the columns might be:

  • First Name.
  • Last Name.
  • Score.

To create an HTML table:

Step 1. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 2. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 3. Press Tab and choose Table.

Step 4. Press enter.

Step 5. Type the table caption and press Enter.

The caption is important because it summarises the purpose of the table for screen-reader users.

Step 6. Type the column headers separated by commas, such as:

First Name,Last Name,Score

Step 7. When all the columns are added, press Enter.

Step 8. Now type the information for the rows. Each cell will be separated by a comma, such as:

Jane,Jones,200

Step 9. When you are ready to enter the information for the next row, press enter.

Step 10. Type the next row as before, with each cell being separated by a comma, like this:

Bary,Johnson,150

Step 11. Repeat the process until all the rows have been added.

Step 12. When the table is complete, press Tab to reach the OK Button and press Enter or Space.

HTML Block Quotes.

A block quote is used for quoted material or text which should be set apart from the surrounding paragraph.

Step 1. Select the quoted text if it has already been written.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Block Quote from the list.

Step 5. Press enter.

Step 6. Type the text if you had not selected it previously. Then Tab to Insert and press Enter or Space

HTML Images.

An image on a web page should include alternative text. Alternative text is the short description a screen-reader user receives when encountering the image.

When creating an HTML image, Leasey Word may ask for:

  • The image source or path.
  • The alternative text.
  • The width.
  • The height.

The image source might be a file path or a location on your web site, such as:

/images/logo.jpg

The alternative text should describe the image in a useful way. For example:

Hartgen Consultancy logo

If the image is important to the page, make the alternative text meaningful. If the image is decorative, consider whether it should be included at all.

You should ask a sighted person to check the final visual result of a web page containing images.

HTML CSS Style Block.

A CSS style block controls how an HTML page is displayed.

This is useful if you want a simple starting point for fonts, spacing, links, tables and block quotes without writing all the CSS yourself.

To insert a CSS style block:

Step 1. Move to the place where the style block should be inserted. In a full HTML document, this is usually in the head section.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose CSS Style Block.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts a basic CSS style block. It uses the current font and point size as a starting point where possible.

You can then edit the CSS directly if you need different colours, spacing, borders or font choices.

Full HTML Document.

The Full HTML Document option is useful when you are starting a new standalone web page.

It can insert the basic structure needed for an HTML page, including the page title and body area.

This option is usually not needed if you are writing inside a blogging system, content management system or form field where the surrounding page structure already exists.

To create a full HTML document:

Step 1. Open a new document or move to the place where the HTML document structure should be inserted.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Full HTML Document.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. Type the document title and press Enter.

Step 7. Type the body text and press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts the basic HTML document structure.

HTML Table of Contents.

For a long web page, a table of contents can help readers move quickly to the section they need.

In HTML, this is usually done by creating links near the top of the page and matching anchor points or IDs near the headings lower down the page.

Leasey Word can help create those links and targets.

Leasey Word will scan the HTML headings and build the table of contents for you.

Step 1. Create your HTML document with heading tags.

Step 2. Move to the place where the table of contents should be inserted.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 4. Choose HTML in the Format Combo Box.

Step 5. Press Tab and choose Build Table of Contents.

Step 6. Press Enter.

Leasey Word scans the heading tags, such as Heading 1 through to Heading 6, creates a linked table of contents, and adds IDs where necessary.

JAWS should announce:

HTML table of contents inserted followed by the number of items.

Markdown Components.

When the Format Combo Box is set to Markdown, the Component List can include items such as:

  • Heading 1 through to Heading 6.
  • Bold.
  • Italic.
  • Bold and italic.
  • Inline code.
  • Code block.
  • Link.
  • Email link.
  • Numbered list.
  • Bulleted list.
  • Block quote.
  • Image.
  • Table.
  • Footnote.
  • Build Table of Contents.
  • Horizontal rule.

Markdown is plain text. This means you can read the formatting characters with JAWS and Braille.

For example, a Markdown heading is marked with number signs. A Markdown link contains the visible text and the web address. A Markdown table uses text characters to show rows and columns.

Markdown Table of Contents.

For a longer Markdown document, a table of contents can help readers move quickly to the heading they need.

Leasey Word can scan Markdown headings, such as Heading 1 through to Heading 6, and create a linked table of contents.

Step 1. Create your Markdown document using headings.

Step 2. Move to the place where the table of contents should be inserted.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 4. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 5. Press Tab and choose Build Table of Contents.

Step 6. Press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts a Markdown list of links to the headings in the document.

JAWS should announce:

Markdown table of contents inserted followed by the number of items.

Markdown Headings.

Step 1. Move to the place where the heading should be inserted, or select the existing heading text.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose the heading level you want.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. If text had not been previously selected, type it and press Enter.

After a Markdown heading, press Enter twice to create the next ordinary paragraph.

When in Quick Navigation Mode:

  • Pressing H and Shift+H will move forward and back by heading.
  • Pressing numbers 1 through to 6, or Shift+1 through to Shift+6, will move forward and back by the chosen heading level.
Markdown Bold, Italic and Code.

Bold and italic are useful for emphasis.

Inline code is useful when referring to a command, filename, variable name or short piece of code within a sentence.

A code block is useful for a longer command, script fragment or example where exact text matters.

Step 1. Select the text if it has already been written.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Bold, Italic, Bold and Italic, Inline Code or Code Block.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. Type or confirm the text if asked to do so.

Step 7. Press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts the required Markdown characters.

Markdown Links.

A Markdown link consists of visible link text and the destination address.

Step 1. Type the visible link text, such as Hartgen Consultancy.

Step 2. Select that text.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 4. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 5. Press Tab and choose Link and press Enter.

Step 6. Type or paste the web address and press Enter.

Leasey Word changes the selected text into a Markdown link.

Markdown Email Links.

A Markdown email link is similar to a web link, but the destination is an email address.

Step 1. Type or select the visible link text, such as Email technical support.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Email Link.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. Type the email address, such as support@hartgenconsultancy.com, and press Enter.

Leasey Word changes the selected text into a Markdown email link.

Markdown Lists.

Markdown supports numbered and bulleted lists.

Use numbered lists for procedures. Use bulleted lists for choices, features or examples.

To create a Markdown list as you write:

Step 1. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 2. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 3. Press Tab and choose Numbered List or Bulleted List.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Step 5. Type each list item on a separate line.

Step 6. Press Tab to reach OK and press Enter or Space.

To convert existing text into a Markdown list:

Step 1. Write each item on its own line.

Step 2. Select the lines.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 4. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 5. Press Tab and choose Numbered List or Bulleted List.

Step 6. Press Enter.

Leasey Word applies the Markdown list structure to the selected lines.

Markdown Tables.

Markdown tables are useful when you want a simple table that remains readable as plain text.

Before creating the table, decide how many columns you need and what the column headings should be.

For example:

  • First Name.
  • Last Name.
  • Total.

Step 1. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 2. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 3. Press Tab and choose Table.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Step 5. Type the column headers separated by commas, such as:

First Name,Last Name,Score

Step 6. When all the columns are added, press Enter.

Step 7. Now type the information for the rows. Each cell will be separated by a comma, such as:

Jane,Jones,200

Step 8. When you are ready to enter the information for the next row, press enter.

Step 9. Type the next row as before, with each cell being separated by a comma, like this:

Bary,Johnson,150

Step 10. Repeat the process until all the rows have been added.

11. When the table is complete, press Tab to reach the OK Button and press Enter or Space.

When reviewing a Markdown document in Quick Navigation Mode, T moves to the next Markdown table and Shift+T moves to the previous Markdown table.

Markdown Images.

A Markdown image contains alternative text and an image source.

The alternative text is important because it describes the image for a screen-reader user.

Step 1. Type or select the alternative text for the image.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Image.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Step 6. Type or paste the image source or URL and press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts the Markdown image reference.

Markdown Footnotes.

Footnotes allow you to place additional explanation at the end of a document while keeping the main text easier to read.

For example, you may want to add a reference, a side note or an explanation without interrupting the main sentence.

Step 1. Move to the point in the text where the footnote reference should appear.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Footnote.

Step 5. A footnote number is offered. You can change it or leave it at the suggestion which is available.

Step 6. Press Enter and type the text for the footnote.

Step 7. Press Tab to reach the OK Button and press Enter or Space.

Markdown Horizontal Rule.

A horizontal rule can be used to separate one part of a document from another.

Step 1. Move to the place where the horizontal rule should be inserted.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+H.

Step 3. Choose Markdown in the Format Combo Box.

Step 4. Press Tab and choose Horizontal Rule.

Step 5. Press Enter.

Leasey Word inserts the Markdown horizontal rule.

Previewing as HTML.

When you are writing HTML or Markdown, source text alone does not always tell you how the finished document will behave.

Preview as HTML lets you open a rendered version in your default browser.

This is useful for checking:

  • Heading structure.
  • Links.
  • Lists.
  • Tables.
  • Paragraph breaks.
  • Block quotes.
  • Images.
  • The table of contents.

To preview the current document:

Step 1. Ensure the document you wish to preview is open.

Step 2. Open the File menu with Alt+F.

Step 3. Press Down Arrow until you reach Preview as HTML.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Leasey Word creates a temporary HTML preview and opens it in the default browser.

If the current document is Markdown, Leasey Word uses the Markdown preview so that Markdown headings, links, lists and tables are rendered properly.

If the document has not yet been saved, Leasey Word can still preview Markdown text in the editor. This is useful if you are drafting a GitHub issue, forum post, blog note or other Markdown content which you intend to paste somewhere else.

JAWS should announce:

HTML preview opened

Previewing does not replace careful checking of the source. It gives you another way to understand the structure of the finished document.

Exporting Markdown as HTML.

If you have written a Markdown document, you may want to create an HTML version for a web page or online resource.

Step 1. Ensure the Markdown document is open.

Step 2. Open the File menu with Alt+F.

Step 3. Press Down Arrow until you reach Export Markdown as HTML.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Step 5. Using standard Windows file browsing techniques, choose the save location.

Step 6. Press Enter to save.

JAWS should announce:

Markdown HTML exported

You can then open the HTML file in a browser and review the result.

Exporting Markdown as Word.

You may also want to create a Microsoft Word document from Markdown.

This is useful if you have written the document efficiently as plain text but need to distribute it as a Word file, edit it in Word, or send it to someone who does not work with Markdown.

Step 1. Ensure the Markdown document is open.

Step 2. Open the File menu with Alt+F.

Step 3. Press Down Arrow until you reach Export Markdown as Word.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Step 5. Using standard Windows file browsing techniques, choose the save location.

Step 6. Press Enter to save.

JAWS should announce:

Markdown Word document exported

A Suggested Workflow.

If you are creating a web page or structured document in Leasey Word, a sensible workflow is:

Step 1. Write the main text first.

Step 2. Use Document and Writing Tools to mark headings, links, lists, tables and other components.

Step 3. Save the document in the appropriate format, such as HTML or Markdown.

Step 4. Use Preview as HTML to check the rendered structure.

Step 5. Return to Leasey Word and correct anything which does not appear as expected.

Step 6. Preview again if necessary.

Step 7. Export the document if you need a separate HTML or Word version.

This approach gives you the accessibility and editing power of Leasey Word while still producing structured documents which can be used elsewhere.

Direct Writing Tool Shortcuts.

If you already know which component you want, you do not always need to open the full Document and Writing Tools dialog.

  • Several commonly used tools have direct shortcuts.
  • - Control+Alt+K inserts or wraps a link.
  • - Control+Alt+1 inserts or wraps a Heading 1.
  • - Control+Alt+2 inserts or wraps a Heading 2.
  • - Control+Alt+3 inserts or wraps a Heading 3.
  • - Control+Alt+4 inserts or wraps a Heading 4.
  • - Control+Alt+5 inserts or wraps a Heading 5.
  • - Control+Alt+6 inserts or wraps a Heading 6.
  • - Control+Shift+H opens Document and Writing Tools, where you can choose a table.
  • - Control+Alt+B inserts or wraps a bulleted list.
  • - Control+Alt+N inserts or wraps a numbered list.
  • - Control+Alt+Q inserts or wraps a block quote.
  • - Control+Alt+I inserts an image.
  • - Control+Alt+H inserts a horizontal rule.

If the current document is HTML, Leasey Word creates HTML.

If the current document is Markdown, Leasey Word creates Markdown.

If the document has not been saved yet, or if Leasey Word cannot tell which format you want, it asks you to choose HTML or Markdown. That choice is remembered for the current open document.

Braille Files.

Leasey Word can open and export Braille files.

The supported Braille file extensions are:

  • BRF.
  • BRL.

This feature uses the Liblouis Braille translator which is installed with JAWS.

Leasey Word does not ship its own separate Braille translator.

Opening a Braille File.

When you open a BRF or BRL file, Leasey Word asks how the file should be opened.

The choices are:

  • Print text.
  • Braille cells.

Print text is the default choice.

If you choose Print text, Leasey Word attempts to back-translate the Braille file into ordinary text.

This means you can use normal Leasey Word commands such as Find, Find Next, copy, word count, bookmarks and other text navigation commands.

This is especially useful if you have a Braille file and want to search for a word or phrase inside it.

To open a Braille file as print text:

Step 1. Press Control+O.

Step 2. Choose the BRF or BRL file and press Enter.

Step 3. When the Open Braille File dialog appears, leave Print text selected.

Step 4. Press Enter.

Leasey Word opens the file as ordinary text where possible.

There is an important point to understand.

A Braille file is already laid out for Braille reading. When it is back-translated into print text, the original print paragraph layout may not be recoverable.

For that reason, the text may not contain the same line breaks or paragraph breaks as the original print document.

However, it should be searchable.

Opening as Braille Cells.

If you choose Braille cells, Leasey Word preserves the Braille-cell representation of the file.

This is useful if you want to read the file on a Braille display in a form closer to the original Braille layout.

To open a Braille file as Braille cells:

Step 1. Press Control+O.

Step 2. Choose the BRF or BRL file and press Enter.

Step 3. In the Open Braille File dialog, press Down Arrow to choose Braille cells.

Step 4. Press Enter.

In Braille cells mode, normal text Find is not expected to work in the same way.

This is because the document is being shown as Braille cells rather than ordinary print letters.

As a general rule:

Choose Print text if you want to search, copy or work with the words as text.

Choose Braille cells if you want to review the Braille layout itself.

Exporting a Document as Braille.

Leasey Word can export the current document to a Braille file.

This is useful if you have written or edited a document and want to move it to a Braille notetaker or another device which can read BRF files.

To export a document as Braille:

Step 1. Open or write the document in Leasey Word.

Step 2. Open the File menu with Alt+F.

Step 3. Press Down Arrow until you reach Export as Braille.

Step 4. Press Enter.

The Export as Braille dialog appears.

The dialog contains:

  • Braille code Combo Box.
  • Output format Combo Box.
  • Line length Spin Box.
  • OK and Cancel Buttons.

The Braille code choices are:

  • UEB contracted.
  • UEB uncontracted.
  • US English contracted.
  • US English uncontracted.
  • UK English contracted.
  • UK English uncontracted.

The output format choices are:

  • BRF Braille ASCII.
  • Unicode Braille cells.

BRF Braille ASCII is usually the best choice if the file is to be used on a Braille notetaker.

The Line length control determines how many Braille cells are placed on each line.

The default is 40.

Step 5. Choose the Braille code you want.

Step 6. Press Tab to choose the output format.

Step 7. Press Tab to set the line length if required.

Step 8. Press Tab to reach OK and press Enter or Space.

Step 9. Choose the folder and file name using the standard Windows Save dialog.

Step 10. Press Enter to save.

JAWS should announce:

Exported Braille file followed by the file name.

Example: Sending a Document to a Braille Notetaker.

Suppose you have written a meeting agenda in Leasey Word and want to read it on a Braille notetaker.

Step 1. Write the agenda in Leasey Word.

Step 2. Open the File menu and choose Export as Braille.

Step 3. Choose the Braille code you prefer, for example UK English contracted.

Step 4. Choose BRF Braille ASCII.

Step 5. Leave the line length at 40 unless your device requires something different.

Step 6. Save the file.

Step 7. Copy the BRF file to the Braille notetaker.

The notetaker should then be able to open the BRF file as a Braille document.

Dictation and Live Transcription.

Dictation allows you to write in the current Leasey Word document by speaking. You can use it to compose a letter, write an email, prepare an article, record your thoughts or add a few sentences to an existing document.

You speak a phrase, pause, and Leasey Word inserts the recognised text. By default, JAWS then reads the inserted phrase back to you, including the names of its punctuation signs. You can check what was recognised before continuing.

You do not have to dictate the whole document. You can combine dictation with ordinary typing, keyboard corrections, reading and navigation.

There is also a separate feature called Live Transcription. This is intended for collecting meeting notes or other continuous speech. It keeps listening through silences and inserts the recognised text without reading each phrase aloud.

The three speech shortcuts can be changed through the Dictation Hotkeys Button on the Dictation tab in Options. See Changing the Dictation Hotkeys below. The defaults are used throughout this documentation.

The main keystrokes are:

  • Control+Alt+D turns Dictation on or off.
  • Control+Alt+T turns Live Transcription on or off.
  • Control+Alt+V opens Dictation Vocabulary Context for the current document.
  • Control+Comma opens Options. Once Options is open, Control+Shift+5 selects the Dictation tab.

Dictation and Live Transcription are also available on the Tools menu. Only one of these two speech features can run at a time.

If you have not used dictation before, begin with the microphone advice and practice exercise below. There is no need to learn all the spoken commands before dictating your first sentence.

How Dictation works.

In order to use dictation, you should have an active internet connection. Similar applications have chosen to use a local AI model in order to process the text. We have deliberately chosen not to do this. Our tests have shown that local models are not anywhere near as accurate as the results in Leasey Word’s dictation feature. This is based upon over 20 years of experience working with voice recognition technology used in conjunction with JAWS in the most demanding of situations.

The dictation feature of Leasey Word does not give you the ability to control your computer by voice, such as that which Dragon NaturallySpeaking provides. If you need that ability, this is not the feature for you. Dragon NaturallySpeaking and our J-Say software are ideally suited to that purpose.

Choosing and Positioning a Microphone.

A noise cancelling headset microphone is essential. Use the headset’s headphones for JAWS speech as well as its microphone for dictation. If you do not have a noise cancelling headset microphone, it is strongly recommended that you do not use this dictation feature. Very often, the speech from JAWS can be captured by the microphone causing extraneous words and phrases to be entered into the document. If you are unable to see the text which has been inadvertently entered into the document, there is a high possibility that you could distribute text to other people which you did not intend. Disabling echo back of dictation is not an adequate substitute. If a Windows notification arrives, or JAWS speaks additional on-screen information, that can be captured by the microphone causing unnecessary text to be inserted. We can recommend a suitable noise cancelling headset microphone.

Using the built-in microphone as part of a laptop computer is not recommended.

When choosing equipment, look for noise cancellation on the microphone. Noise cancellation in the headphones alone does not describe how well the microphone rejects sounds in the room.

Position the microphone near your mouth, slightly to one side so you are not breathing directly into it. Positioning the microphone two fingers width away from your mouth is a good starting point. Keep it in a consistent position and speak at a comfortable, ordinary volume. You should not need to shout or pronounce every word in an exaggerated way.

Choose a quiet place where possible. Television, radio, another conversation or someone speaking near the microphone can become part of the recognised text.

To select your microphone in Leasey Word:

Step 1. Connect the microphone or headset before opening Options.

Step 2. Press Control+Comma.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+5 to select the Dictation tab.

Step 4. Move to the Microphone source Combo Box. Use the Arrow keys to select the microphone you want.

Step 5. Press Enter to save the settings.

Windows default microphone follows the input selected as the Windows default. Selecting a named microphone makes it easier to be certain which input you are using when several are connected.

The list shows the available Windows recording inputs. Some audio interfaces provide several input pairs, so more than one entry can belong to the same physical device.

Selecting a microphone here does not change the audio source for the JAWS speech. Make sure JAWS is also using the headset’s headphones. If JAWS is still coming from loudspeakers, correct that before beginning your practice.

If a previously selected microphone is shown as unavailable, reconnect it or choose an available input. The same microphone selection is used by Dictation and Live Transcription.

Your First Dictated Sentence.

Step 1. Open a blank document with Control+N.

Step 2. Press Control+Alt+D.

Step 3. Wait until JAWS says “Dictation on”. This tells you that listening has started.

Step 4. Speak the following sentence at a natural pace, without naming its punctuation:

This morning I went for a walk in the park

Step 5. Pause at the end of the sentence. Do not press Enter to submit it. Leasey Word detects the pause and waits for the recognised text.

An example of the result is:

This morning, I went for a walk in the park.

The punctuation is supplied automatically. The exact punctuation can vary; Leasey may decide, for example, that a comma is unnecessary.

With the default confirmation setting, JAWS reads the inserted text back and names its punctuation. For the example above, you would hear:

This morning comma I went for a walk in the park Full-stop

The words “comma” and “Full-stop” are part of the spoken confirmation. The document contains the punctuation characters, not those words. A Braille display shows the document text with its actual punctuation.

Step 6. After the confirmation has finished, dictate another sentence and pause again.

Step 7. When you have finished, press Control+Alt+D. JAWS says “Dictation off”.

If a phrase is still being processed, it can arrive after this announcement. “Dictation off” means that listening has stopped; it does not mean that every previously recorded word has already been inserted. Let the final phrase arrive before closing the document, opening another document or starting another speech session.

Step 8. Review the text with the usual reading keys and save it with Control+S.

Speak Up to a Natural Punctuation Break.

The most useful habit to develop is to think about what you want to say, then speak up to a point where punctuation would naturally belong. A complete sentence is a good starting point.

Leasey considers the words in each phrase and supplies punctuation and capitalisation. A noticeable pause can tell Leasey Word that you have finished a phrase, even if you intended to continue the same sentence.

For example, try to say “This morning I went for a walk in the park” as one phrase, then pause. If you say only “This morning”, stop to think, and later say “I went for a walk in the park”, the service may treat these as separate statements and punctuate them accordingly.

You do not need to speak rapidly or hold your breath. Speak comfortably, giving Leasey enough of a thought to understand. If a long sentence is difficult, consider expressing it as two shorter sentences.

Avoid deliberately pausing after every word. Dictation works best when it can recognise the relationship between words in a phrase.

You can dictate several sentences together once you feel comfortable. To begin with, one sentence followed by a pause gives you a useful opportunity to listen to the result and correct any mistakes.

There is a short interval between your pause and the returned text. The time can vary with the connection and the service. A brief wait does not necessarily mean that the microphone has stopped working.

During your early practice, wait for the confirmation before speaking the next phrase. This makes it easier to learn the rhythm of speaking, pausing and checking.

Dictating in English and Spanish.

The Dictation languages Combo Box offers two choices: English, which is the default, and English and Spanish. Choose English when you intend to dictate in English only. Choose English and Spanish if you want to dictate in Spanish or move between English and Spanish.

Choosing English and Spanish enables Leasey Word’s full set of Spanish punctuation and formatting commands. It gives you the following additional controls:

  • Use translated editing commands such as “tachar eso”, “todo en mayúsculas”, “activar modo deletreo” and “Leasey seleccionar”, as described in Spanish Editing Commands below.
  • Say Spanish punctuation names, such as “coma”, “punto” and “abrir interrogación”, to request the corresponding punctuation marks.
  • Use Spanish punctuation names in Spell Mode, alongside the English letter and number names. For example, “bravo arroba charlie punto delta” inserts “b@c.d”.
  • Say “nueva línea” to start a new line, or “nuevo párrafo” to start a new paragraph. “Nueva línea” also continues or ends a numbered list when Automatic numbering is enabled. Switch Spell Mode off before using these line and paragraph commands.

English punctuation names and commands remain available with English and Spanish selected. You can use either set of punctuation names without changing the setting each time.

You can also change languages as you speak, including within the same phrase. You do not need a command or keystroke each time you change language. The text follows the language spoken; this setting does not translate it.

Step 1. If Dictation or Live Transcription is listening, stop it and wait for the final phrase to arrive.

Step 2. Press Control+Comma to open Options.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+5 to select the Dictation tab.

Step 4. Press Tab until you reach the Dictation languages Combo Box.

Step 5. Use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to choose English and Spanish.

Step 6. Press Tab until you reach the OK Button, then press Enter. Your choice is remembered when Leasey Word restarts. Press Escape instead if you want to discard the change.

Step 7. Start Dictation with Control+Alt+D and wait for “Dictation on”. Speak in English, Spanish, or a mixture of the two.

For example, you could say “Good morning, María”, then continue “¿Cómo estás?”. Review the resulting text in the usual way, including accents and punctuation.

The service may recognise Spanish speech or interpret a Spanish punctuation name even with English selected. However, that does not enable the full set of Spanish commands in Leasey Word. To use the Spanish commands described in this guide, including those in Spell Mode, choose English and Spanish.

Spanish editing commands are also available for removing the last phrase, changing capitalisation, switching Spell Mode, copying the document, inserting Markdown markers, and moving to or selecting text. English commands remain available. The pause setting works in the same way for both languages. The complete Spanish punctuation and editing-command lists appear below.

This language setting applies to Dictation only. It does not change Live Transcription, the spelling dictionary, or your JAWS voice settings. Return to English in this Combo Box when you want English-only dictation again.

Allowing More Time to Pause.

The recommended pause before processing a phrase is 0.6 seconds. This is the default and gives the quickest response when you finish speaking. We recommend keeping this setting for everyday dictation and speaking up to a natural punctuation break.

If you need more time to think within a sentence, you can choose a longer pause. For example, with a two-second pause selected, you can briefly stop after “This morning”, then continue “I went for a walk in the park” before the two seconds have elapsed. The words remain part of the same phrase. Each time you resume speaking, the pause starts counting again when you next stop.

The Pause before processing a phrase Combo Box offers 0.6 seconds, 1 second, 1.5 seconds, 2 seconds, 2.5 seconds, 3 seconds, 3.5 seconds, 4 seconds, 4.5 seconds and 5 seconds. The 0.6-second choice is marked “recommended”.

Step 1. If Dictation or Live Transcription is listening, stop it and wait for the final phrase to arrive.

Step 2. Press Control+Comma to open Options.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+5 to select the Dictation tab.

Step 4. Press Tab until you reach the Pause before processing a phrase Combo Box.

Step 5. Use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to choose the pause you want. You could try 1.5 or 2 seconds if you need a little more thinking time.

Step 6. Press Tab until you reach the OK Button, then press Enter. Your choice is saved and remembered when you restart Leasey Word. Press Escape instead if you want to discard the change.

Step 7. Press Control+Alt+D to start Dictation, wait for “Dictation on”, and try a sentence using your chosen pause.

A longer setting means a longer wait after you finish a phrase, followed by the time needed to return the text. It also means waiting longer after a spoken command such as “new paragraph” or “forget it”. Allow the selected pause to pass and the result to arrive before speaking a separate command or phrase. If the wait feels too long, return to a shorter value; 0.6 seconds remains our recommendation.

This setting allows more time within a phrase. It does not turn off automatic punctuation or guarantee where punctuation will be placed. The service still considers the words you have spoken. The setting applies to Dictation only; it does not change Live Transcription.

Pressing Control+Alt+D to stop Dictation finishes the recorded phrase without waiting for the selected pause. Allow time for that phrase to be returned and inserted.

Automatic Punctuation and Spoken Punctuation.

You do not have to name every punctuation sign. Dictation normally adds punctuation and capitalisation, and attempts to remove fillers and apply self-corrections. Review the result because it may not be a word-for-word record of everything you said.

For example, if you correct yourself while speaking, Leasey may keep the corrected version rather than both versions. If you are collecting a discussion rather than composing your own text, consider Live Transcription, described below.

You can also speak the names of punctuation signs when you want to indicate them explicitly. Examples include:

  • Comma.
  • Full-stop, or period.
  • Question mark.
  • Exclamation mark.
  • Colon.
  • Semicolon.
  • Open parenthesis and close parenthesis.

Say the punctuation name as part of the phrase. For example:

Hello comma how are you question mark.

The intended result is:

Hello, how are you?

For the earlier practice sentence, you could say:

This morning comma I went for a walk in the park Full-stop

You can use “period” in place of “Full-stop”. Both are intended to produce the same character. An ordinary use of the word, such as “a trial period”, should remain part of the sentence.

Speaking a punctuation name gives the service a more explicit indication of what you want. It does not turn off automatic punctuation elsewhere in the phrase. There is currently no setting which guarantees that punctuation will be added only where you have spoken its name but we expect this to be available in the coming months.

Punctuation and phrase cleanup are automatic. There is no checkbox to turn either off. The Dictation tab in Options contains the microphone, custom words, confirmation, pause and language settings.

Always review punctuation where its exact placement matters. If Leasey adds a Full-stop or period where you wanted to continue a sentence, you can remove it with the keyboard and continue writing.

Spanish Punctuation Commands.

Spanish punctuation names are available only when English and Spanish is selected in the Dictation languages Combo Box. The English punctuation names remain available in this mode too. With English selected, use English punctuation commands. Stop Dictation before changing the language setting, then start it again to use the new choice. Speak the punctuation name as part of your phrase, or say it on its own after the previous phrase has finished. For example, say “Querida Belinda coma” for “Querida Belinda,”. Say “Abrir interrogación cómo estás cerrar interrogación” for “¿Cómo estás?”.

The following commands and alternatives are available:

  • Full stop / period: say “Punto”. Inserts `.`.
  • Comma: say “Coma”. Inserts `,`.
  • Colon: say “Dos puntos”. Inserts `:`.
  • Semicolon: say “Punto y coma”. Inserts `;`.
  • Opening question mark: say “Abrir interrogación”. Inserts `¿`.
  • Closing question mark: say “Cerrar interrogación”. Inserts `?`.
  • Opening exclamation mark: say “Abrir admiración” or “Abrir exclamación”. Inserts `¡`.
  • Closing exclamation mark: say “Cerrar admiración” or “Cerrar Exclamación”. Inserts `!`.
  • Hyphen: say “Guion”. Inserts `-`.
  • Long dash: say “Guión largo”. Inserts `—`.
  • Opening parenthesis / round bracket: say “Abrir paréntesis”. Inserts `(`.
  • Closing parenthesis / round bracket: say “Cerrar paréntesis”. Inserts `)`.
  • At sign: say “Arroba”. Inserts `@`.
  • Dot / decimal point: say “Punto” or “Punto Decimal”. Inserts `.`.
  • Underscore: say “Guion bajo” or “Guión al piso”. Inserts `_`.
  • Apostrophe / single quotation mark: say “Apóstrofo”. Inserts `’`.
  • Double quotation mark: say “Comillas dobles” or “Comillas”. Inserts `“`.
  • Forward slash: say “Barra”. Inserts `/`.
  • Backslash: say “Barra invertida”. Inserts `\.
  • Ampersand: say “Y comercial”. Inserts `&`.
  • Hash / number sign: say “Numeral”. Inserts `#`.
  • Dollar sign: say “Signo de dólar” or “Signo de Pesos”. Inserts `$`.
  • Pound sterling sign: say “Signo de libra esterlina”. Inserts `£`.
  • Euro sign: say “Signo de euro”. Inserts `€`.
  • Percent sign: say “Por ciento”. Inserts `%`.
  • Plus sign: say “Más”. Inserts `+`.
  • Minus sign: say “Menos”. Inserts `-`.
  • Equals sign: say “Igual”. Inserts `=`.
  • Asterisk: say “Asterisco”. Inserts `*`.
  • Opening square bracket: say “Abrir corchete”. Inserts `[`.
  • Closing square bracket: say “Cerrar corchete”. Inserts `]`.
  • Opening brace / curly bracket: say “Abrir llave”. Inserts `{`.
  • Closing brace / curly bracket: say “Cerrar llave”. Inserts `}`.
  • Less-than sign: say “Menor que”. Inserts `<`.
  • Greater-than sign: say “Mayor que”. Inserts `>`.
  • Vertical bar / pipe: say “Barra vertical”. Inserts `|`.
  • Tilde symbol: say “Virgulilla”. Inserts `~`.
  • Caret symbol: say “Acento circunflejo”. Inserts `^`.
  • New line: say “Nueva línea”.
  • New paragraph: say “Nuevo párrafo”.

“Nueva línea” works like “new line”, including continuing or ending a numbered list when Automatic numbering is enabled. “Nuevo párrafo” works like “new paragraph” and leaves a blank line between paragraphs.

With English and Spanish selected, Spanish punctuation names also work in Spell Mode, alone or between English letter and number names. For example, “cap bravo arroba charlie punto delta” inserts “B@c.d”, without adding spaces. Switch Spell Mode off before using the line-break and paragraph-break commands. Letter and number names remain in English. Translated editing commands are listed in the following section.

Some names, such as “más”, “menos”, “igual” and “punto”, are also ordinary Spanish words. Within a sentence, the surrounding wording helps distinguish them from punctuation commands. Saying one of these names on its own requests the symbol. In ordinary Dictation, say “literal” before a command name when you want its words inserted instead; for example, “literal coma” inserts “coma”.

Spanish punctuation commands do not turn off automatic punctuation. Review the result in the usual way. With spoken confirmation enabled, punctuation is named aloud and the document and Braille output retain the actual characters.

Spanish Editing Commands.

Choose English and Spanish in the Dictation languages Combo Box to use the following commands. The English commands remain available too. These commands work during Dictation; in Live Transcription they are treated as ordinary speech.

Say the commands for switching modes, removing the last phrase and copying the document as a phrase on their own. Wait for the result before continuing. Confirmation messages remain in English.

  • Forget It: say “Tachar eso” or “Borrar eso”. Removes the last dictated phrase and reports the current sentence, or Blank if no sentence remains.
  • Capitalise the initial letter: say “Mayúscula inicial” followed by the word. For example, “mayúscula inicial él” inserts “Él”. In Spell Mode, use it before the letter name; “mayúscula inicial bravo” inserts “B”.
  • Capitalise one whole word: say “Palabra en mayúsculas” or “Toda la palabra en mayúsculas”, followed by the word. For example, “palabra en mayúsculas árbol” inserts “ÁRBOL”.
  • All Caps On: say “Todo en mayúsculas”. Subsequent dictated phrases are inserted in capital letters.
  • All Caps Off: say “Desactivar mayúsculas”. Returns subsequent phrases to normal capitalisation.
  • Spell Mode On: say “Activar modo deletreo”.
  • Spell Mode Off: say “Desactivar modo deletreo”.
  • Insert Before: say “Leasey insertar antes del” or “Leasey insertar antes de”, followed by the text to find. For example, “Leasey insertar antes de María” moves the cursor immediately before María.
  • Insert After: say “Leasey insertar después del” or “Leasey insertar después de”, followed by the text to find. For example, “Leasey insertar después de María” moves the cursor immediately after María.
  • Select Text: say “Leasey seleccionar”, followed by the text to select. For example, “Leasey seleccionar buenos días” selects the first matching occurrence of buenos días.
  • Copy Document: say “Copiar todo en el portapapeles” or “Copiar documento”. Copies all the text of the current document to the clipboard.
  • Heading One: say “Encabezado uno”. Inserts one hash sign followed by a space.
  • Heading Two: say “Encabezado dos”. Inserts two hash signs followed by a space.
  • Heading Three: say “Encabezado tres”. Inserts three hash signs followed by a space.
  • Heading Four: say “Encabezado cuatro”. Inserts four hash signs followed by a space.
  • Heading Five: say “Encabezado cinco”. Inserts five hash signs followed by a space.
  • Heading Six: say “Encabezado seis”. Inserts six hash signs followed by a space.
  • Bullet Text: say “Texto con viñeta” or “Insertar viñeta”. Inserts a dash followed by a space. Begin on a new line when inserting a heading or bullet.
  • Space in Spell Mode: say “Barra espaciadora” or “Espacio”. Inserts a space between the spelled characters.
  • Literal Command: say “Comando literal”, followed by the command words. For example, “comando literal copiar documento” inserts “copiar documento” without copying the document. Use this outside Spell Mode.
  • New Line: say “Nueva línea”. Continues or ends a numbered list when Automatic numbering is enabled.
  • New Paragraph: say “Nuevo párrafo”. Leaves a blank line between paragraphs.

Spell Mode continues to use English letter names, English phonetic words and English number names. The translated Spell Mode controls, capitalisation command, space commands and Spanish punctuation names can be used with them. For example, “mayúscula inicial bravo espacio two” inserts “B 2”.

Switch Spell Mode off before using headings, bullets, line and paragraph breaks, Copy Document, or the commands for finding and selecting text. All Caps On, All Caps Off and Forget It remain available in Spell Mode.

Leasey Clip and Leasey Text keep their existing English command names. Keep the word Leasey at the beginning of the translated Insert Before, Insert After and Select commands.

What Is Self-Correction?.

As the name suggests, self-correction as where you correct yourself if you have made a mistake. We often do this as part of natural speech. For example, you might say: “We will meet on Tuesday, no, Wednesday at three o’clock.”

Leasey Word is able to handle self-corrections. However, for accurate dictation, you are advised not to do this if it can be avoided. In the above example, Leasey Word attempts to remove the abandoned choice, “Tuesday”, and the correction word, “no”. Make the correction within the same spoken phrase, without a long pause. If the earlier phrase has already been processed and inserted, this feature does not go back and revise it. You would instead use “forget it” (described below) or edit the existing text.

Choosing How Dictated Text Is Confirmed.

Open Options with Control+Comma, then press Control+Shift+5. Move to Dictation confirmation.

The choices are:

  • Echo phrase by phrase. This is the default. JAWS reads each inserted phrase and speaks punctuation names, helping you check the result as you write. In most cases this setting is recommended. If Leasey Word has entered punctuation signs where they were not required, this is the ideal way of being able to confirm that and make an immediate correction. If it has inserted unwanted punctuation signs, and you have not enabled this option, you cannot blame the application. You have specifically elected not to use this setting.
  • Play sound. A sound indicates that text has been inserted, without reading the phrase aloud.
  • No Confirmation. Leasey Word inserts the phrase without its own spoken confirmation or insertion sound. You can review the document using your usual reading keys or Braille display. If you are using the JAWS speech output only rather than Braille, this setting has a particular disadvantage. You will not be aware that the text has finished processing.

Use the Arrow keys to choose the confirmation you prefer, then Tab to OK and press Enter.

This setting controls the feedback after inserting a phrase. It does not change whether Leasey adds punctuation. Turning off confirmation also does not change your general JAWS settings or prevent the microphone from hearing speech produced by other commands.

For a new user, Echo phrase by phrase is a useful way to check both recognition and punctuation. If using this option, keep JAWS speech in your headphones so that the microphone does not hear the result being read back. If necessary, reduce the volume of JAWS by pressing Control+Windows+Shift+Down Arrow.

Live Transcription always inserts its phrases quietly, regardless of this dictation confirmation setting.

Changing the Dictation Hotkeys.

You can change the three shortcuts for Dictation, Live Transcription and Dictation Vocabulary Context. This is useful if another program, JAWS or your own preferred key assignments already use one of them. The shortcuts given elsewhere in this documentation are the defaults. If you change one, use your chosen shortcut in its place.

Step 1. If Dictation or Live Transcription is listening, stop it and wait for the final phrase to arrive.

Step 2. Press Control+Comma to open Options.

Step 3. Press Control+Shift+5 to select the Dictation tab.

Step 4. Press Tab until you reach the Dictation Hotkeys Button, immediately after Custom Dictation Words. Press Enter to open it.

Step 5. Focus is in the Dictation hotkey Edit Field, with the current shortcut selected. Type the shortcut you want, for example F8 or Control+Alt+F8. Type the letters, numbers and plus signs as text; do not press the key combination itself. Control can also be written as Ctrl.

Step 6. Press Tab to reach the Live Transcription hotkey Edit Field. Change this shortcut if required.

Step 7. Press Tab to reach the Dictation Vocabulary Context hotkey Edit Field. Change this shortcut if required.

Step 8. Press Tab to reach the Restore Defaults Button. To keep your changes, leave this button alone and press Tab again to reach OK. Press Enter to return to the Dictation tab in Options.

Step 9. Focus returns to the Dictation Hotkeys Button. Press Tab until you reach the OK Button in Options, then press Enter to save your changes.

JAWS says “Options saved”. The new shortcuts now work and are remembered when you close and reopen Leasey Word. The Tools menu and Leasey Command Centre show your chosen keys.

You can use a letter or number with Control or Alt, optionally including Shift. You can also use a function key, such as F8, on its own or with Control, Alt or Shift. A shortcut must not already be assigned to another Leasey Word command. Windows-key combinations are not available here.

If a shortcut is invalid, already used by Leasey Word, or assigned to two of these speech commands, a message explains the problem. Close the message with Enter. Focus returns to the relevant Edit Field with its contents selected, ready for you to type a different shortcut. Choose OK again when you have corrected it.

To remove a shortcut, clear its Edit Field and choose OK, then choose OK in Options. The command remains available on the Tools menu, so you can still start and stop Dictation or Live Transcription without a shortcut.

To restore the original three shortcuts, press the Restore Defaults Button, choose OK, then choose OK in Options. The defaults are Control+Alt+D for Dictation, Control+Alt+T for Live Transcription, and Control+Alt+V for Dictation Vocabulary Context.

Press Escape or choose Cancel in the hotkeys dialog to return to Options without accepting those changes. Choosing Cancel in Options discards all changes made there, including any hotkeys you have just accepted. Restore Defaults is also only saved when you choose OK in both dialogs.

Control+Shift+I reports your location in the dialog. Control+Alt+Z gives help.

These shortcuts work while you are using Leasey Word. Leasey Word checks its own assignments, but cannot detect every shortcut used by JAWS or another program. If a chosen key is intercepted elsewhere, return to this dialog and choose another combination.

Starting, Stopping and Taking a Break.

Control+Alt+D is a toggle. Press it once to start dictation and again to stop. The corresponding item on the Tools menu is checked while dictation is listening.

Wait for “Dictation on” before speaking. Pressing the shortcut while the connection is still starting can stop that attempt, so give it time to become ready.

If no speech is detected for 30 seconds, dictation stops automatically and announces this. Press Control+Alt+D again when you are ready to continue. Your existing text remains in the document.

If you want to think, talk to someone else or read a long passage with JAWS, stop dictation yourself first. The microphone cannot distinguish a comment to another person from words intended for the document.

Before changing documents, opening Options or vocabulary settings, or turning on Read Only Mode, stop dictation and let the final phrase finish. Those actions cancel listening and any results still pending. They do not remove text already inserted.

Opening another Leasey Word dialog while a phrase is being processed can also stop dictation. If a result arrives while a dialog is open, Leasey Word can present it in a read-only dialog so you can copy the phrase instead of losing access to it. Return to the document before restarting dictation.

Where the Text Is Inserted.

Leasey Word inserts each returned phrase at the current cursor position in the document where you started dictation. It does not always add text to the end of the document.

If text is selected when the phrase arrives, the recognised words replace that selection. This lets you select an incorrect word or sentence and dictate its replacement.

To add text at the end of a document, press Control+End before dictating. To add text elsewhere, move the cursor to the required position first. Make sure you have not left an unwanted selection active.

You can make keyboard corrections or move the cursor between phrases without ending the dictation session. Remember, however, that a phrase still being processed will use the cursor position and selection present when it arrives. Let the current phrase finish before moving somewhere else if that is not where you want those words inserted. Remember also that producing vocal utterances as you make corrections could be interpreted as words. While this is a natural thing to do, if you are unable to see the contents of the document you could find that unwanted words or phrases could form part of the text.

For your first few sessions, it may be easier to dictate a sentence, listen to it, stop dictation, make any corrections, and then start again. You can combine speaking and keyboard work more freely as you become familiar with the feature.

New Lines and Paragraphs.

Say “new line” to move to the next line, or “new paragraph” to insert a paragraph break with a blank line.

For practice, dictate a complete sentence and let it arrive. Then say “new paragraph” as a phrase on its own and pause. With spoken confirmation enabled, JAWS says “New paragraph”. You can then dictate the first sentence of the next paragraph.

These are dictation commands. The words “new paragraph” are not inserted into the document when the command is recognised.

If you want the actual words, say “literal new paragraph”. The word “literal” tells Leasey Word to treat the following recognised command as text.

Dictating Markdown Headings and Bullets.
