You can dictate Markdown heading and bullet markers. These commands insert ordinary text at the cursor. Start on a new line, using “new line” if needed, before adding a heading or bullet.

  • “Heading one” inserts one hash sign followed by a space.
  • “Heading two” inserts two hash signs followed by a space.
  • “Heading three” inserts three hash signs followed by a space.
  • “Heading four” inserts four hash signs followed by a space.
  • “Heading five” inserts five hash signs followed by a space.
  • “Heading six” inserts six hash signs followed by a space.
  • “Bullet text” inserts a dash followed by a space.

Say the command and pause, then dictate the heading or bullet wording. The space after the marker is included automatically. With spoken confirmation enabled, a command on its own is announced as “Heading 2”, for example, or “Bullet text”.

You can also include the wording in the same phrase. For example, “Heading two Meeting notes” produces:

## Meeting notes

“Bullet text Bring a notebook” produces:

Bring a notebook.

To write the command’s words instead, say “literal heading two” or “literal bullet text”. You can use “forget it” to undo the most recent insertion.

These commands apply to Dictation. Live Transcription treats them as ordinary spoken words.

Specifying Capital Letters.

Normal sentence capitalisation is automatic. When you need to specify a capital letter, say “cap” immediately before the word in the same phrase.

For example:

Today I went for a walk in the cap park.

The command asks Leasey Word to begin “Park” with a capital P. The word “cap” is not inserted.

Say “all caps” immediately before a word to put that whole word into capital letters:

Today I went for a walk in the all caps park.
  • Here, “park” becomes “PARK”.
  • These two commands apply to the following word. For several words or phrases in capitals, use “all caps on” and “all caps off”, described below. You can also select existing text and use the Upper Case command, Control+Alt+U.

Keep the command and its word together. Saying “cap”, pausing until it is processed, and then saying the word does not carry the capitalisation instruction over to the next phrase.

Leasey Word handles these capitalisation commands itself. If you need the word “cap” as ordinary text, say “literal cap”. Always review names and abbreviations where the exact capitalisation matters.

Keeping All Caps On Across Phrases.

Enabling and disabling capital letters is a little like pressing the Caps Lock key on a computer keyboard. Say “all caps on” as a complete phrase by itself, then pause. JAWS confirms “All caps on”. The command itself does not insert any text.

From that point, each subsequent dictated phrase is inserted in capital letters. You can dictate several sentences or paragraphs without repeating the command. Punctuation and phrase cleanup still take place; Leasey Word capitalises the resulting text before inserting it.

For example:

Step 1. While Dictation is listening, say “all caps on” and pause for the confirmation.

Step 2. Dictate:

Please keep this door closed full stop.

The intended result is:

PLEASE KEEP THIS DOOR CLOSED.

Step 3. Continue dictating if you want more text in capitals. A “new line” or “new paragraph” command does not switch the capitals mode off.

Step 4. Say “all caps off” as a complete phrase on its own, then pause. JAWS confirms “All caps off”. Subsequent phrases use normal capitalisation again.

Keep each mode command separate from the text you want to dictate. Use “all caps on”, pause, then speak the text. Use “all caps off” in the same way when you have finished the capitalised passage.

The mode affects newly dictated text. It does not change text already in the document or switch on the keyboard’s Caps Lock setting. The shorter command “all caps” immediately followed by a word remains available when you only want that one word capitalised.

All caps mode lasts for the current dictation session. Each new session starts with all caps off, including when you restart after the 30-second silence timeout. If you stop dictation while a phrase is still being processed, that final phrase retains the capitalisation mode which applies to it.

To insert the words of a mode command without changing the setting, say “literal all caps on” or “literal all caps off” as a phrase on its own. Those words are inserted using the current capitalisation mode.

These are Dictation commands. In Live Transcription, “all caps on” and “all caps off” are ordinary speech and do not change the capitalisation mode.

Spell Mode.

Spell Mode lets you dictate individual letters, numbers and punctuation, for example when entering a name, an email address, an abbreviation or a reference number. You can use ordinary letter names or the phonetic alphabet. Letters are lowercase by default. Say “cap” immediately before a letter to make that letter a capital, and say “space” wherever you want a space.

Step 1. Press Control+Alt+D to start Dictation and wait until you hear “Dictation on”.

Step 2. Say “spell mode on” as a complete phrase on its own. Pause until JAWS confirms “Spell mode on”.

Step 3. Speak the letters, digits or punctuation names you want. For example:

bravo delta zero seven

This inserts:

bd07

You can also say “B D zero seven”. If similar-sounding letters are difficult to recognise, use phonetic words such as Bravo for B and Delta for D.

Step 4. To capitalise an individual letter, say “cap” and the letter together in the same phrase. For example:

cap bravo romeo india alpha november space two

This inserts:

Brian 2.

Only the letter following “cap” is capitalised. You can repeat “cap” before another letter when needed. The separate “all caps on” and “all caps off” commands also remain available if you deliberately want a whole sequence of capital letters.

Step 5. Continue spelling as needed. You can pause between groups of letters. Each group is joined to the previous group without an automatic space or punctuation mark. Say “space” to insert one space, either by itself or between other letters in the same phrase. You can also type a space using the keyboard.

Punctuation can be spoken on its own or between letters. For example:

bravo at sign charlie period delta echo

This inserts:

b@c.de

Say “at sign” for @. Say “period”, “full stop” or “dot” for a full-stop, and “comma” for a comma. No spaces are added around punctuation. You can pause before and after a punctuation name, just as you can between groups of letters.

Other supported names include:

  • Hyphen or dash; underscore; apostrophe; single quote; double quote.
  • Colon; semicolon; question mark; exclamation mark.
  • Forward slash or slash; backslash; ampersand; hash sign or number sign.
  • Dollar sign; pound sign; euro sign; percent sign; plus sign; equals sign; asterisk or star.
  • Open parenthesis; close parenthesis; open square bracket; close square bracket; open brace; close brace.
  • Less than; greater than; vertical bar; tilde; caret.

Spell Mode still avoids automatic sentence punctuation between letters. If a spoken punctuation name is missed, try saying it as a separate phrase and check the echoed character.

Step 6. When you have finished spelling, say “spell mode off” as a complete phrase on its own and pause. JAWS confirms “Spell mode off”. You can then dictate ordinary sentences again. Switching Spell Mode off does not change the separate All Caps setting.

The phonetic alphabet is:

Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliet, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu.

For numbers, say the individual digits: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Leading zeros are retained. Say “zero” for the digit 0 and “Oscar” for the letter O when you need to distinguish them. “Oh” is treated as the letter O. “Double U” is the letter W.

Your usual dictation confirmation choice still applies. With spoken confirmation selected, the characters are read individually; capital letters and spaces are identified, and punctuation names such as “at sign”, “full stop” and “comma” are spoken. With Play Sound or No Confirmation selected, that choice is respected.

If a phrase contains something Spell Mode cannot interpret, JAWS says “Spelling not understood. Nothing inserted. Try letter names or phonetic words.” None of that phrase is inserted, and you can repeat it. Review important names and codes because speech recognition can still mistake one valid letter or digit for another.

“Forget it” remains available to remove the last inserted group. If you replaced selected text, it restores that text. Other dictation commands should be used after switching Spell Mode off.

Spell Mode is remembered until you say “spell mode off”. Stopping and restarting Dictation, including after the 30-second silence timeout, preserves your choice. The setting is also remembered when you close and reopen Leasey Word. When Dictation starts with Spell Mode enabled, JAWS announces “Dictation on, spell mode on” once the microphone is ready. With Spell Mode disabled, it announces “Dictation on”. Spell Mode is off initially until you first enable it.

It uses English letter names and phonetic words even if English and Spanish dictation is selected. In Live Transcription, “spell mode on” and “spell mode off” are ordinary speech. Outside Spell Mode, say “literal spell mode on” or “literal spell mode off” to insert those words themselves.

Removing the Last Dictated Phrase.

If the most recent phrase is wrong and you want to try again, say “forget it” on its own and pause.

Leasey Word removes the last dictation insertion and announces “Last phrase removed”, followed by the current sentence at the cursor. If the cursor is on an empty line, or the document is empty, it says “Blank”. If that insertion replaced selected text, the earlier selected text is restored and the sentence containing it is read.

This command is intended for an immediate correction. It is not a general command for undoing any earlier action in the document. If you have changed the text since that insertion, or there is no suitable last phrase, Leasey Word says “Nothing to forget”.

After the removal, speak the replacement phrase. If you have already made other corrections, use the normal keyboard editing commands instead.

To insert the words “forget it” rather than carry out the command, say “literal forget it”.

Copying the Document by Voice.

While dictation is listening, say “Copy Document” as a complete phrase, with nothing else, and pause.

Leasey Word copies all the text in the current document to the Windows Clipboard and says “Document copied”. You do not have to select the text first. This copies the document text, not the document file or its formatting.

The document and cursor position stay as they are, and dictation continues. If you want to move to another application and paste the result, stop dictation first and let any pending phrase finish.

The complete phrase is required. A longer sentence which merely mentions copying a document does not activate the command.

To write the words “Copy Document” into the document, say “literal Copy Document” as a phrase on its own.

Moving to Existing Text by Voice.

Three commands can help you return to words already in the document:

  • Say “Leasey insert before”, followed by the words to find, to put the cursor before them.
  • Say “Leasey insert after”, followed by the words to find, to put the cursor after them.
  • Say “Leasey select”, followed by the words to find, to select them.

Speak the command and the words to find in one phrase, then pause. For example:

Leasey select a walk in the park.

If those words are found, Leasey Word announces “Phrase selected”. Your next dictated phrase replaces that selection.

For the two insertion commands, Leasey Word announces “Insertion point moved”. The next phrase is inserted at the new position.

The search uses the first matching occurrence in the document. If the same words appear more than once, include enough surrounding words to identify the passage you need, and check the position before replacing text. If nothing matches, you hear “Phrase not found”.

You can still use the ordinary Find and navigation commands. Stop dictation and let the last phrase finish before opening a Find dialog.

Inserting a Saved Leasey Text.

If you already use Leasey Texts for frequently used wording, you can insert one by saying “Leasey Text”, followed by its saved name.

For example, if you have a Leasey Text named “Business signature”, say:

Leasey Text Business signature.

Speak this as one phrase and pause. Leasey Word inserts the saved text at the current cursor position, replacing any selected text.

The Leasey Text must already exist. Its Enable abbreviation checkbox does not need to be checked when inserting it by voice. If its name cannot be found, or the words match more than one saved entry, Leasey Word tells you. Use a distinctive saved name to make recognition and matching easier.

Inserting a Leasey Clip.

If you use Leasey Clips to store text for pasting later, you can paste any of the twelve clips by voice while dictation is listening. The clip must already have been stored using Leasey, and JAWS and Leasey must be running.

Keep Leasey Word in the foreground, with the cursor where you want to insert the clip. If text is selected, the clip replaces that selection in the usual way.

Say “Leasey Clip”, followed by the number from one to twelve, as a complete phrase and then pause. For example:

Leasey Clip 1.
Leasey Clip 6.
Leasey Clip 12.

Speak the numbers normally. It does not matter whether dictation recognises the number as a word, such as “one”, or as a digit, such as “1”.

Leasey Word calls the existing Leasey JAWS script for that clip, just as when using the clip’s keyboard command. The usual Leasey Clip behaviour and feedback apply. The spoken command itself is not inserted into the document or echoed back as a dictated phrase. Wait for the paste to finish before continuing to dictate.

All Caps mode does not change the contents of a Leasey Clip. To undo a clip paste, use the normal Undo command. “Forget it” is for removing dictated text and does not undo a Leasey Clip command.

To write the command words into your document, say “literal Leasey Clip one”. Mentioning “Leasey Clip one” within a longer sentence does not paste the clip. In Live Transcription, these commands are treated as ordinary speech.

Helping Dictation Recognise Names and Specialist Words.

Ordinary vocabulary will often be recognised without any preparation. Names, company names, specialist terms and unusual spellings may benefit from a little extra information.

There are two ways to supply this information: Custom Dictation Words, and Dictation Vocabulary Context. They serve different purposes, and both are shared with Live Transcription.

Custom Dictation Words is a saved list of words or short phrases which you want the service to recognise. Use it for recurring names and terms across different documents.

To add an entry:

Step 1. Stop dictation and let the final phrase finish.

Step 2. Open the Tools menu and choose Custom Dictation Words. You can also reach it through the button on the Dictation tab in Options.

Step 3. In the Word or phrase Edit Field, type the spelling you want the service to recognise. For example, type a colleague’s surname or a product name.

Step 4. Press Enter, or Tab to the Add Button and press Space. The word is added to the list, and the Edit Field is cleared ready for another entry.

Step 5. Add any further words you need. To remove an entry, select it in the Custom words list and activate Remove.

Step 6. Activate OK to save the list. If you opened it from Options, also activate OK in Options to save the changes there.

Step 7. Start dictation again to use the updated list.

You can save up to 100 entries, with a maximum of 50 characters in each. An entry can be a short phrase, not just a single word. Adding a term improves the information available to the service; it does not guarantee the spelling on every occasion.

Dictation Vocabulary Context describes the subject of the current document. Use this when the topic changes, for example when moving from a letter about a holiday to notes about specialist software. You do not have to do this, but it can help since Leasey has some proposed context to work with. If you do not change the proposed vocabulary, the results are still exceptionally accurate.

To set the context:

Step 1. Stop dictation and let the final phrase finish.

Step 2. Press Control+Alt+V.

Step 3. Type a brief description of the subject and any useful background. For example:

Notes about accessible software, JAWS screen reader commands, Braille displays and Leasey Word.

Step 4. Move to OK and press Enter.

Step 5. Start dictation again.

The description is not inserted into your document. It gives Leasey background which may help it choose between words that sound similar.

Describe the subject rather than using this field for editing commands or instructions such as “do not add punctuation”. It is a vocabulary aid, not a replacement for the punctuation behaviour described earlier.

The context belongs to the current open document and lasts while that document remains open. It is not remembered when you close and reopen the document. Custom Dictation Words, by contrast, are saved for future use across documents.

You can press Control+Alt+V again to change or clear the description. Keep it concise. Live Transcription uses only its first 1750 characters, because its recognition service has a shorter context limit.

Using Live Transcription for Meeting Notes.

Dictation is designed for composing your own text, with phrase confirmation and spoken editing commands. Live Transcription is designed to keep collecting speech over a longer discussion.

Normal transcription punctuation and capitalisation can still appear. It is not a way to guarantee an exact, unpunctuated record, and you should still review the recognised words.

To start:

Step 1. Open an editable document, or create a new one for the notes.

Step 2. Choose the required microphone and vocabulary settings before starting. These are the same settings used for dictation.

Step 3. Position the cursor where you want the transcript to begin.

Step 4. Press Control+Alt+T, or choose Live Transcription from the Tools menu.

Step 5. Wait for “Live transcription on”.

Step 6. Let the discussion continue. Completed phrases are inserted into the document as the service returns them. You do not have to wait until the meeting ends to receive the text.

Step 7. Press Control+Alt+T again to stop. JAWS says “Live transcription off”. Let the final phrase arrive before leaving the document or starting dictation.

Step 8. Review and save the notes.

Unlike dictation, Live Transcription does not stop after 30 seconds of silence. It also does not read each inserted phrase aloud or play the dictation confirmation sound. This avoids Leasey Word’s phrase feedback speaking over the discussion.

Spoken editing commands are ordinary content in this mode. If a participant says “Copy Document”, “forget it”, “new paragraph” or “all caps”, Leasey Word does not execute those words as a command. Use the keyboard for any editing you need.

Live Transcription captures the selected recording input. It does not automatically capture the other participants in an online meeting just because their voices are audible through your headphones. Check your audio arrangement with a short test so you know which voices reach the selected input. A headset microphone intended to pick up your voice may not be suitable for everyone seated around a meeting table.

The same document protections apply as for dictation. Switching or closing the document, opening Options or vocabulary settings, or enabling Read Only Mode cancels listening and pending results. Stop with Control+Alt+T and let the final phrase finish first.

Only one speech mode can run at a time. To move from Live Transcription to Dictation, stop Live Transcription, wait for its final phrase, then press Control+Alt+D. To go the other way, stop Dictation and let it finish before pressing Control+Alt+T.

Live Transcription produces a transcript. It does not automatically turn the discussion into a summary or minutes. After stopping and reviewing the text, you can use the ChatGPT Text Tools described earlier in this chapter to help prepare a meeting summary or extract action items.

If the Result Is Not What You Expected.

If no words appear, first check that you heard “Dictation on” or “Live transcription on”. Confirm that the correct microphone is selected, that it is not muted, and that your internet connection is available. A document in Read Only Mode cannot receive dictated text.

If JAWS feedback appears in the document, stop listening and check that JAWS is being played through your headphones. Make sure the microphone is not picking up loudspeakers or another nearby device. Choosing Play sound or No Confirmation can reduce phrase feedback while you check the arrangement, but it does not stop other JAWS speech from reaching the microphone.

If unexpected Full-stops or capitals appear in the middle of your intended sentence, consider where you paused. Try speaking through to the next natural punctuation break. If you need more thinking time within the sentence, try a longer Pause before processing a phrase in Dictation Options, as described in Allowing More Time to Pause. The recommended setting remains 0.6 seconds. You can speak punctuation names explicitly, but automatic punctuation may still be added.

If a name is repeatedly wrong, check that you are speaking clearly and that the microphone is well positioned. Add the name to Custom Dictation Words, or use Control+Alt+V to describe the subject. Stop and restart the speech feature after changing these settings.

If the wrong passage is replaced, check whether it was selected when the phrase arrived. Dictation replaces the current selection. When moving around the document, let a pending phrase finish before selecting a different passage.

If dictation turns off while you are thinking, remember the 30-second silence limit. Press Control+Alt+D to start again. For a meeting where longer silences are expected, use Live Transcription.

If a spoken command is inserted as text during Live Transcription, that is expected. Spoken editing commands belong to Dictation. Stop Live Transcription and start Dictation if you want to use those commands.

If the service reports an error, review the end of the document before repeating your last sentence. Some text may already have been inserted. Restart listening after addressing the reported problem, and repeat only what is missing.

A Suggested Practice Session.

Step 1. Use your headset, check the microphone selection, and leave Echo phrase by phrase enabled.

Step 2. Open a blank document and start Dictation with Control+Alt+D.

Step 3. Dictate the walk-in-the-park sentence as one natural phrase. Pause and listen to the words and punctuation.

Step 4. Say “new paragraph” on its own and pause.

Step 5. Dictate another sentence, this time speaking “comma” or “Full-stop” where you want those signs.

Step 6. After the sentence has arrived, say “forget it” on its own. Listen for “Last phrase removed”, followed by the current sentence or “Blank”, then dictate a replacement sentence.

Step 7. Say “Copy Document” on its own. Listen for “Document copied”.

Step 8. Stop Dictation, let the last result finish, and read through the document using your usual JAWS or Braille reading commands.

Step 9. Save the document if you want to keep it.

Once these steps are comfortable, try capitalisation commands, custom vocabulary and a short Live Transcription session. You can introduce each feature gradually while continuing to use the keyboard whenever it is more convenient.

AutoCorrect.

AutoCorrect replaces common typing mistakes using a saved list of words and their replacements. For example, typing “teh” followed by Space changes it to “the”. Typing “recieve” followed by Space changes it to “receive”.

Leasey Word supplies more than 200 starter entries. You can change these entries, remove any you do not want, and add your own. The list is stored locally with your Leasey Word settings. AutoCorrect itself does not need an internet connection.

AutoCorrect uses the replacements in this list. It does not automatically choose the spell checker’s first suggestion, check grammar, or rewrite a sentence. Commonly confused words such as “form” and “from” are not automatically exchanged. British and American spellings such as “colour” and “color” are left as they are.

Turning AutoCorrect On and Choosing Feedback.

Step 1. Press Control+Comma to open Options.

Step 2. With Options open, press Control+Shift+6 to select AutoCorrect. Focus moves to the “Auto-correct as you type” Combo Box.

Step 3. Use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to choose one of the following three settings:

  • Off. No automatic corrections are made.
  • Play sound. Common typing mistakes are corrected, and a sound confirms each correction.
  • Say corrected. Common typing mistakes are corrected, and JAWS says “Corrected” each time. No correction sound is played.

Step 4. Press Tab until you reach the OK Button.

Step 5. Press Enter to save the setting and return to your document.

AutoCorrect is Off by default. Your choice is remembered when Leasey Word is restarted. To turn it off, return to the same Combo Box, select Off, and choose OK. If you already had AutoCorrect turned on, it continues with Play sound until you change the setting.

What Happens While Typing.

Finish a word by pressing Space, Enter, or typing punctuation such as a full-stop or period, comma, question mark, exclamation mark, colon or semicolon. If the completed word has an applicable entry, Leasey Word replaces it and leaves you ready to continue typing.

Corrections preserve the usual capitalisation. For example, “teh” becomes “the”, “Teh” becomes “The”, and “TEH” becomes “THE”. Words containing an unusual mixture of upper and lower case are left alone. A replacement can contain more than one word: “alot” becomes “a lot”.

Each automatic correction either plays the AutoCorrect sound or says “Corrected”, according to your choice in Options. The Say corrected setting does not read out the replacement word. JAWS continues to provide its usual typing feedback. Moving back over a corrected word does not announce “AutoCorrect” or offer an extra command.

AutoCorrect acts on words you are typing. Opening a document, pasting text or moving through existing text does not automatically correct that text. Use F7 to review spelling in existing text.

Undoing a Correction.

If a correction is unwanted, press Control+Z immediately after it happens. The original word is restored, with the word-ending space or punctuation retained, and the cursor is ready to continue typing. The restored word is not immediately corrected again. Control+Y can redo the correction.

If you have continued typing, normal Undo order applies to those later edits first. To prevent a particular correction in future, remove or change its entry as described below.

AutoCorrect and Live Spelling Alerts.

AutoCorrect acts before Live Spelling Alerts. When “teh” is changed to “the”, you hear the selected AutoCorrect feedback: a sound or “Corrected”. There is no additional sound or spoken spelling alert for that word.

If a word has no applicable AutoCorrect entry, Live Spelling Alerts can still check it and either play its usual sound or say “Misspelled”, according to the mode selected with Control+Shift+M.

You can use either feature independently. Turning Live Spelling Alerts off does not turn AutoCorrect off or silence its selected feedback. Turning AutoCorrect off leaves Live Spelling Alerts available as usual.

The supplied corrections respect the spelling dictionary, personal dictionary and words ignored for the current document. An explicit replacement you add yourself can override an accepted dictionary word. This allows deliberate personal replacements without automatically changing names or specialist vocabulary.

Managing the Entries.

You can add your own corrections, change the replacement for an existing entry, or remove an entry you do not want.

Step 1. Press Control+Comma to open Options.

Step 2. Press Control+Shift+6 to select the AutoCorrect page.

Step 3. Press Tab until you reach the Manage AutoCorrect entries Button.

Step 4. Press Enter or Space Bar to open the AutoCorrect Entries dialog.

The focus is now on the AutoCorrect entries List Box. Use Up Arrow and Down Arrow to review the entries. Each entry gives the word to be replaced followed by its replacement.

The dialog has two Edit Fields. Replace contains the incorrect word. With contains the word or phrase which should be inserted instead. These are the names JAWS announces.

Adding a New Entry.

Begin in the AutoCorrect Entries dialog described above. This example adds “becaues” as a mistake to be replaced by “because”.

Step 1. Press Tab until you reach the New entry Button.

Step 2. Press Enter or Space Bar. The two Edit Fields are cleared and the focus moves automatically to the Replace Edit Field.

Step 3. Type the incorrect word, “becaues”, without the quotation marks.

Step 4. Press Tab once to move to the With Edit Field.

Step 5. Type the replacement, “because”, without the quotation marks.

Step 6. Press Tab once to reach the Add or update Button.

Step 7. Press Enter or Space Bar. You hear “AutoCorrect entry updated”, and the focus returns to the List Box with your entry selected.

You can repeat these steps to add another entry. When you have finished, follow Saving Your Changes below.

Replace must contain one word; apostrophes are allowed. With can contain a word or short phrase on one line. The limits are 80 characters for Replace and 240 characters for With.

If the word in Replace already has an entry, Add or update changes that entry’s replacement instead of creating a duplicate.

Changing an Existing Entry.

Step 1. In the AutoCorrect entries List Box, use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to select the entry you want to change.

Step 2. Press Tab once to reach the Replace Edit Field. Leave this word unchanged if you want to keep correcting the same mistake.

Step 3. Press Tab once to reach the With Edit Field.

Step 4. Type the new replacement word or phrase.

Step 5. Press Tab once to reach the Add or update Button.

Step 6 Press Enter or Space Bar. You hear “AutoCorrect entry updated”, and the focus returns to the List Box.

When you have finished making changes, follow Saving Your Changes below.

If you change the word in the Replace Edit Field, Add or update creates or updates the entry for that different word. The original entry remains in the list until you remove it.

Removing an Entry.

Step 1. In the AutoCorrect entries List Box, use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to select the entry you want to remove.

Step 2. Press Delete. Alternatively, press Tab until you reach the Remove Button, then press Enter or Space Bar.

Step 3. A confirmation dialog asks whether you want to remove the selected entry. The Yes Button has focus.

Step 4. Press Enter or Space Bar to confirm. You hear “AutoCorrect entry removed”, and the focus returns to the List Box. To keep the entry instead, press Tab to the No Button and press Enter or Space Bar.

Step 5. Follow Saving Your Changes below to keep the removal.

You can remove both supplied entries and entries you added yourself. Removing an entry stops that automatic replacement in future. It does not alter text already corrected in a document.

Restoring the Supplied Entries.

Step 1. In the AutoCorrect Entries dialog, press Tab until you reach the Restore starter entries Button.

Step 2. Press Enter or Space Bar. A confirmation dialog asks whether you want to restore all supplied entries.

Step 3. To continue, move to the Yes Button with Tab and press Enter or Space Bar. To leave your entries unchanged, choose No.

Step 4. After restoring the entries, follow Saving Your Changes below.

Restoring the starter entries brings back any supplied entries you removed and resets changes made to their replacements. Your other custom entries are retained.

Saving Your Changes.

There are two OK Buttons to use: one in the AutoCorrect Entries dialog and one in Options.

Step 1. In the AutoCorrect Entries dialog, press Tab until you reach the OK Button.

Step 2. Press Enter or Space Bar. The Entries dialog closes, and you return to the Manage AutoCorrect entries Button in Options.

Step 3. Press Tab until you reach the OK Button in Options.

Step 4. Press Enter or Space Bar. Options closes and your changes are saved.

If you edited the Replace or With fields but did not activate Add or update, the Entries dialog’s OK Button also checks and accepts that edit.

Pressing Escape in the Entries dialog cancels changes made in that dialog. Pressing Escape in the main Options dialog discards changes made during that Options visit, including entries you accepted with the first OK Button. Adding an entry does not turn AutoCorrect on. Select Play sound or Say corrected in the Auto-correct as you type Combo Box on the AutoCorrect page in Options if you want your entries to be applied while typing.

Adding an Entry from Spell Check.

You can save a correction as an AutoCorrect entry while checking a document with F7.

Step 1. Press F7 to open Spell Check. When a misspelled word is found, the focus moves to the Suggestions List Box.

Step 2. Use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to select the replacement you want. Do not press Enter yet: Enter on a suggestion changes the current occurrence without adding an AutoCorrect entry.

Step 3. Press Tab to reach the Replacement Edit Field. It contains the selected suggestion. If this is the replacement you want, leave it unchanged. To enter a different replacement, press Control+A and type the word or phrase you want instead.

Step 4. Press Tab until you reach the Add to AutoCorrect Button.

Step 5. Press Enter or Space Bar. Leasey Word saves the replacement as an AutoCorrect entry, changes the current occurrence, and continues the spell check.

The existing Change and Change All Buttons make spelling corrections without creating AutoCorrect entries. The Add Button adds the original word to the personal spelling dictionary; it does not create a replacement rule.

Adding an entry does not automatically enable AutoCorrect. Select Play sound or Say corrected in the Auto-correct as you type Combo Box in Options when you want to use the entries. An entry saved from Spell Check remains saved even if you later cancel the spell-check session.

Where AutoCorrect Is Avoided.

AutoCorrect is unavailable in Read Only mode. It skips recognised web addresses, email addresses, file paths, code and Markdown code blocks. It is also disabled for source-code, configuration and Braille file types. Ordinary prose in Markdown can still be corrected.

The supplied list is intended for UK and US English. Custom entries can be used with other languages. Review your entries if an intended word is repeatedly changed; an explicit rule is a personal instruction to replace that word.

Options.

Open Options with Control+Comma.

Options is divided into tabbed pages so related settings are grouped together.

To move quickly to an Options tab:

  • Press Control+Shift+1 for Opening and Saving.
  • Press Control+Shift+2 for Speaking and Display.
  • Press Control+Shift+3 for ChatGPT.
  • Press Control+Shift+4 for Data and File Explorer.
  • Press Control+Shift+5 for Dictation.
  • Press Control+Shift+6 for AutoCorrect.
AutoCorrect Tab.

With Options open, press Control+Shift+6. Focus moves to the Auto-correct as you type Combo Box. Use Up Arrow or Down Arrow to choose Off, Play sound, or Say corrected. Off is the default. Press Tab to reach the Manage AutoCorrect entries Button. For setup, correction feedback, Undo, and editing the replacement list, refer to the separate AutoCorrect section above.

Dictation Tab.

With Options open, press Control+Shift+5 to select this tab. Microphone source selects the Windows recording input used by Dictation and Live Transcription.

The Custom Dictation Words Button opens the saved list of names, words and short phrases which you want the service to recognise.

The Dictation Hotkeys Button opens the three shortcut settings for Dictation, Live Transcription and Dictation Vocabulary Context. Choose OK in that dialog, then OK in Options to save your changes. For detailed steps, refer to Changing the Dictation Hotkeys earlier in Part 2.

Dictation confirmation offers Echo phrase by phrase, Play sound, and No Confirmation. Echo phrase by phrase is the default and speaks punctuation names as well as the inserted words. This setting applies to Dictation; Live Transcription always inserts text quietly.

Pause before processing a phrase is a Combo Box. The default and recommended value is 0.6 seconds, which gives the quickest response. Longer values run from 1 to 5 seconds in half-second steps, allowing more thinking time within a phrase. Longer values also delay the returned text and confirmation. The setting is remembered and applies only to Dictation. For detailed steps, refer to Allowing More Time to Pause earlier in Part 2. Dictation languages is a Combo Box offering English, the default, and English and Spanish. Choose English and Spanish to enable the full Spanish punctuation commands, including punctuation in Spell Mode, and the “nueva línea” and “nuevo párrafo” commands. English commands remain available. The combined choice also lets you dictate in either language or switch between them as you speak, without translating the text. The combined choice also enables the Spanish editing commands described in Spanish Editing Commands earlier in Part 2. The choice is remembered and applies to Dictation only. For detailed steps, refer to Dictating in English and Spanish earlier in Part 2.

Punctuation and phrase cleanup are automatic. There are no separate punctuation or cleanup checkboxes.

Choose OK to save your changes. Stop either speech feature and let its final phrase finish before opening Options, then start it again after changing the settings.

For setup, practice exercises, spoken commands, vocabulary context and meeting notes, refer to Dictation and Live Transcription earlier in Part 2.

Opening and Saving Tab.

The Opening and Saving tab contains settings which affect how documents are opened, saved and presented in file dialogs.

Restore last cursor position when opening documents Check Box. When this is checked, Leasey Word returns to the last known cursor position when opening a document you have used before.

This is useful when reading or editing long documents because you do not need to manually find your previous place.

Number of recent files Edit Spinbox.

This controls how many files are kept in the Recent Files list.

The value can be between 5 and 50.

Use this if you frequently return to documents you have recently edited.

Default document save folder Edit Field and Browse Button. This is the folder Leasey Word suggests whenever Save As opens, including when saving a copy of an existing document.

You can type a path or use the Browse Button to choose a folder.

If quotation marks are included, Leasey Word removes them.

If the folder does not exist, Leasey Word tries to create it when Options is saved.

Save As starts in this default folder even if the document was opened from another folder. If no usable default folder is set, it starts in the document’s own folder. Control+S still saves an existing writable document to its current location.

Default save format Combo Box. This controls the file type Leasey Word suggests when saving a new composed document.

The choices are:

  • Text document.
  • Markdown.
  • HTML.
  • Word document.

Text document is the default.

If you choose Word document, new documents will normally be offered as DOCX files when Save As opens.

This setting does not force every document to become that format.

If you open an existing editable file, such as HTML or Markdown, Leasey Word continues to save it in its existing format.

If you open a PDF or another rendered document, Leasey Word still protects the original file and opens Save As.

Suggest first line as file name Check Box. When this is checked, Leasey Word uses the first non-empty line of a new document as the suggested file name when Save As opens.

For example, if the first line is:

Meeting Notes for Friday

The Save dialog will suggest:

Meeting Notes for Friday

Leasey Word removes characters which cannot be used in Windows file names.

This option is useful if you usually begin a document with a title.

Use simplified Open and Save dialogs Check Box. This option is not checked by default.

When unchecked, Leasey Word uses the standard Windows Open and Save dialogs.

When checked, Control+O and Control+Shift+S use simpler Leasey dialogs.

The simplified dialogs contain a Path Edit Field, Folder list, Open or Save Button, and Cancel Button. In the Folder list, use Up Arrow and Down Arrow to move through folders and files.

Press Enter on a folder to open it.

Press Enter on a file to choose it.

Press Backspace to move back one folder.

When you press Backspace, focus returns to the folder you just came out of.

If you are at the root of a drive, such as C:\ pressing Backspace moves to the list of drives.

Press Enter on a drive to open it.

You can type the first few letters of a folder or file name to move to it.

You can also type or paste a full path into the Path Edit Field and press Enter.

Speaking and Display Tab.

The Speaking and Display tab contains settings which affect what Leasey Word shows or announces while you move through a document.

Speak document composition indentation level when moving by line Check Box. When this is checked, Leasey Word announces paragraph formatting indentation changes while you move with Up Arrow and Down Arrow.

This relates to document composition indentation, such as increasing or decreasing paragraph indentation for ordinary writing.

Speak code indentation when moving by line Check Box. When this is checked, Leasey Word announces actual leading spaces and tabs at the start of a line while you move with Up Arrow and Down Arrow.

This is useful when editing code, scripts, configuration files, HTML, PHP or other structured text where indentation is part of the content.

Word wrap Check Box. This option is checked by default.

When checked, long lines wrap within the document window.

When unchecked, long lines continue horizontally.

Turning word wrap off can be useful when editing HTML, source code, log files or other documents where the exact line structure matters.

You can also press Control+Alt+W from the document window to turn word wrap on or off quickly.

Automatic numbering Check Box. This option is unchecked by default. Open Options with Control+Comma, press Control+Shift+2 for Speaking and Display, then Tab to Automatic numbering. Press Space to check it and choose OK. Your choice is remembered when you next use Leasey Word.

To start a numbered list, begin a line with a number, a period and a space, then type the item. For example:

1. First item.

Press Enter at the end of the item. Leasey Word inserts “2.” on the next line, ready for the next item. Type that item and press Enter to continue with “3.”.

You can also use the word Step:

Step 1. Open the document.
Step 2. Make your changes.

After typing the first step, Enter inserts “Step 2.”, and so on. The new number is spoken after Enter, for example “2” or “Step 2”, so you do not need to use JAWS Say Line to check it. You can begin with a different number if needed. Any spaces or tabs before the number, and the capitalisation of Step, are kept on subsequent items.

To finish the list, press Enter twice after the last item’s text. The first Enter inserts the next number. The second Enter removes that empty number, says “List ended”, and leaves a blank line between the last item and the next paragraph. The cursor is ready to type below that blank line. To start a new list from one, type “1.” or “Step 1.” again. A previous list’s count is not carried forward.

Shift+Enter inserts a normal line break without adding a number. Enter within an item’s text, or while text is selected, keeps its normal behaviour. Automatic numbering does not change pasted text or numbers already elsewhere in the document.

During dictation, saying “new line” uses the same numbering rules as Enter. This works both as a phrase on its own and within a longer dictated phrase. For example, if the current line begins “Step 1.”, dictate the first step and say “new line”. Leasey Word inserts “Step 2.”, ready for the next step.

To end the list by voice, say “new line” again while the numbered item is empty. This leaves a blank line before the next paragraph. You can also say “new line new line” after the last item’s text. With spoken confirmation enabled, saying “new line” on its own announces just the new number, such as “2” or “Step 2”. For longer dictated phrases, the automatic numbers are included in the normal echo. Removing an empty number is confirmed as “List ended”. If you have selected Play sound or No Confirmation for dictation, that setting is respected. “Forget it” can undo the whole dictated phrase, including any automatic numbers or removal of an empty number.

“New paragraph” keeps its ordinary behaviour, and “literal new line” inserts those words. These voice commands are not executed in Live Transcription.

The numbers are ordinary document text and are saved with the document. Control+Z can undo an automatic numbering action. Uncheck Automatic numbering whenever you want to type every number yourself.

Announce Leasey Document Notes when moving by line Check Box. This option is checked by default.

When checked, Leasey Word announces the name of a Leasey Document Note when Up Arrow or Down Arrow lands on a line containing one.

The announcement is made using the JAWS Message Voice so it can be distinguished from the line text.

If this option is unchecked, Leasey Word does not announce note names during line-by-line navigation.

You can still use F5 to open the Leasey Document Notes list, F6 to review the note at the current position, and Quick Navigation N or Shift+N to move by notes.

ChatGPT Tab.

The ChatGPT tab contains settings which affect how ChatGPT Text Tools place results into your document.

Review individual ChatGPT changes before applying Check Box. This option is checked by default.

When checked, Leasey Word displays the Review ChatGPT Changes dialog before ChatGPT Text Tools replace text in the document.

This gives you a chance to inspect each proposed change.

You can accept or reject individual changes and then apply the result.

If this option is unchecked, Leasey Word applies ChatGPT replacement results immediately, as it did in earlier versions.

Preview full ChatGPT result before applying Check Box. This option is not checked by default.

When checked, Leasey Word does not immediately replace text when a ChatGPT Text Tool returns replacement text.

Instead, it opens the ChatGPT Replacement Preview dialog.

The dialog contains an editable field called Replacement text.

You can read the result, make any small changes you want, then Tab to Accept and press Enter or Space.

If you press Escape, the document is not changed.

This option is useful if you want to inspect the whole ChatGPT result before it is placed into the document.

Data and File Explorer Tab.

The Data and File Explorer tab contains settings and commands which affect where Leasey Word stores its own data and how it integrates with Windows File Explorer.

Leasey Word data location Edit Field and Browse Button. This controls where Leasey Word stores its settings, document recovery information, bookmarks and other application data.

This will be fully described in the chapter of this documentation relating to the Backup and Restore Manager and should generally not be changed here.

Restore to Location Default Button. This restores the Leasey Word data location to the standard Leasey location.

Use this only if you deliberately changed the data location and want to return to the default.

Register File Explorer entries Button. When activated, this registers Leasey Word with Windows so supported documents can be opened from File Explorer using Leasey Word.

This adds Leasey Word to Windows Open With choices and adds an Open with Leasey Word entry for supported document types.

JAWS should announce:

File Explorer entries registered

Delete formatted files Button. This deletes saved Leasey formatted files from the Formatted Files folder. It does not delete your documents. Use this if you no longer need Leasey Word to restore formatting for plain text files, or if you want to clear the stored formatting information.

Leasey Word asks before deleting the files.

JAWS should announce:

Deleted followed by the number of formatted files.

Supported Formats and Known Limitations.

Leasey Word can currently open and render the following formats as plain text:

  • EPUB.
  • HTML, HTM and XHTML.
  • Markdown formats.
  • DOC, DOCX and DOCM.
  • PDF.
  • PPTX and PPTM.
  • RTF.
  • TXT and LOG.
  • CUE, INI, JCF, JKM, JSON and PHP.
  • XML.

RTF support is basic.

Leasey Word first tries to read RTF documents directly.

If direct reading fails and Microsoft Word is available, Leasey Word may ask Word to read the RTF document as a fallback.

RTF formatting may not be preserved.

Visible hyperlink text and other field results are retained when an RTF document is opened. This includes scripture references, cross-references and similar text. You can read and search these references with the usual reading and Find commands.

Embedded RTF hyperlinks also appear in the Links list. Press JAWS Key+F7, or Control+Alt+F7, to open the list. Use Up Arrow and Down Arrow to choose a link, then press Enter to move to its text in the document. This moves within the document; it does not open the destination website.

Link destinations appear in the Links list without adding long web addresses to the document’s reading text. If a link’s text is removed or changed, it may no longer appear in the list.

Saving the extracted text to another format does not recreate the embedded RTF hyperlinks. The reference text remains readable and searchable in the saved copy. Keep the original RTF document if you want to reopen it with its embedded links.

Older binary PowerPoint files, PPT, are not yet supported.

Keystroke Summary.

General Document Commands.

Leasey Key followed by Windows+W starts Leasey Word.

Control+N creates a new blank document.

Control+Shift+N creates a new document from the Windows clipboard.

Control+O opens a document.

Control+S saves the current document.

Control+Shift+S opens Save As.

Control+P opens the Print dialog.

Control+Alt+W turns word wrap on or off.

Control+F4 closes the current document.

Control+W also closes the current document.

Alt+F4 exits Leasey Word.

Control+F6 moves to the next open document.

Control+Tab also moves to the next open document.

Control+Shift+F6 moves to the previous open document.

Control+Shift+Tab also moves to the previous open document.

Editing Commands.

Control+Z performs Undo.

Control+Y performs Redo.

Control+X cuts selected text.

Control+C copies selected text.

Control+V pastes text.

Control+A selects all text.

Control+Delete deletes the next word.

Control+Backspace deletes the previous word.

The Leasey Key followed by Comma marks the start point for Leasey Select.

The Leasey Key followed by full-stop or period marks the end point for Leasey Select.

Find and Replace.

Control+F finds text.

Control+Shift+F searches backwards.

F3 finds the next occurrence.

Shift+F3 finds the previous occurrence.

Control+H opens Find and Replace.

Document Navigation Lists.

JAWS Key+F6 opens the Headings list.

JAWS Key+F7 opens the Links list.

Case and Formatting.

Control+Alt+U changes selected text, or the whole document, to upper case.

Control+Alt+L changes selected text, or the whole document, to lower case.

Control+Shift+O opens Sort Lines.

Control+Shift+H opens Document Writing Tools.

Control+B toggles bold.

Control+I toggles italic.

Control+U toggles underline.

Control+Shift+Y highlights selected text or removes highlight from selected highlighted text.

Control+Alt+Y opens the Highlighted Items list.

Control+D opens the Font dialog.

Control+L aligns left.

Control+E centres the current line or selection.

Control+R aligns right.

Control+J justifies the current line or selection.

Control+Alt+Right Arrow increases indentation.

Control+Alt+Left Arrow decreases indentation.

Direct Writing Tool Shortcuts.

Control+Alt+K inserts or wraps a link.

Control+Alt+1 inserts or wraps a Heading 1.

Control+Alt+2 inserts or wraps a Heading 2.

Control+Alt+3 inserts or wraps a Heading 3.

Control+Alt+4 inserts or wraps a Heading 4.

Control+Alt+5 inserts or wraps a Heading 5.

Control+Alt+6 inserts or wraps a Heading 6.

Control+Shift+H opens Document and Writing Tools, where you can choose a table.

Control+Alt+B inserts or wraps a bulleted list.

Control+Alt+N inserts or wraps a numbered list.

Control+Alt+Q inserts or wraps a block quote.

Control+Alt+I inserts an image.

Control+Alt+H inserts a horizontal rule.

Spelling.

F7 opens Spell Check.

Tab moves to the next control in the Spell Check dialog.

Shift+Tab moves to the previous control in the Spell Check dialog.

Up Arrow and Down Arrow move through the Suggestions list.

Enter or Alt+C changes the current word when focus is in the Suggestions list.

Enter or Alt+C changes the current word when focus is in the Replacement Edit Field.

Delete or Alt+I ignores the current spelling issue.

Control+R reads the sentence in the Spell Check dialog.

Alt+A activates Change All.

Alt+G activates Ignore All.

Alt+D activates Add.

Alt+F activates Finish.

Escape cancels spell checking.

Control+Alt+E opens the Misspelled Words dialog.

Control+Shift+M cycles Live Spelling Alerts through Off, Play sound, and Say misspelled.

Control+M adds the focused word or selected word to the personal dictionary.

Control+Shift+D removes the focused word or selected word from the personal dictionary.

Alt+Semicolon moves to the next spelling error.

Alt+Apostrophe moves to the previous spelling error.

Alt+Shift+Semicolon moves to the first spelling error.

Alt+Shift+Apostrophe moves to the last spelling error.

Bookmarks, Points and Position.

Control+K sets a Leasey Word bookmark.

Control+Shift+G opens the Bookmarks dialog.

Control+Shift+K sets a temporary bookmark.

Alt+Shift+K moves to the temporary bookmark.

F4 adds a Leasey Document Note at the current position.

F5 opens the Leasey Document Notes dialog.

F6 opens the Leasey Document Note at the current position in a read-only Edit Field, if one is available.

Control+G opens Go To Page.

Page Down moves to the next page marker where page markers exist.

Page Up moves to the previous page marker where page markers exist.

Control+Shift+W opens Word Count.

Control+Shift+I performs Where Am I.

Control+Shift+P speaks the full path of the current document.

The Leasey Key followed by Control+1 through to Control+0 sets Leasey Points 1 through to 10.

The Leasey Key followed by 1 through to 0 moves to Leasey Points 1 through to 10.

Quick Navigation Mode.

Insert+Z turns Quick Navigation Mode on or off.

Caps Lock+Z does the same if using the JAWS laptop keyboard layout.

When Quick Navigation Mode is on:

P moves to the next paragraph.

Shift+P moves to the previous paragraph.

S moves to the next sentence.

Shift+S moves to the previous sentence.

Space moves to the next page marker if available.

Backspace moves to the previous page marker if available.

H moves to the next heading.

Shift+H moves to the previous heading.

1 through to 6 move to the next heading at that level.

Shift+1 through to Shift+6 move to the previous heading at that level.

B moves to the next bookmark.

Shift+B moves to the previous bookmark.

N moves to the next Leasey Document Note.

Shift+N moves to the previous Leasey Document Note.

T moves to the next table.

Shift+T moves to the previous table.

Y moves to the next highlighted item.

Shift+Y moves to the previous highlighted item.

M moves to the next misspelling.

Shift+M moves to the previous misspelling.

Context Menu or Shift+F10 opens spelling suggestions when a misspelling is selected.

Dictation and Live Transcription.

Control+Alt+D starts or stops Dictation. Wait for “Dictation on” before speaking. After stopping, let any final phrase finish inserting.

Control+Alt+T starts or stops Live Transcription for meeting notes. It keeps listening through silences and inserts completed phrases quietly.

Control+Alt+V opens Dictation Vocabulary Context for the current document.

Control+Comma opens Options. With Options open, Control+Shift+5 selects the Dictation tab for microphone, custom words, confirmation, pause and language settings.

The three speech shortcuts above are the defaults. Open Options with Control+Comma, press Control+Shift+5 for Dictation, then choose Dictation Hotkeys to change them, remove an assignment or restore the defaults.

Custom Dictation Words is also available on the Tools menu.

Tools and Application Features.

Control+Shift+C opens Leasey Command Centre.

Control+Shift+T opens ChatGPT Text Tools.

Control+Shift+E opens Translate Text.

Control+Shift+L inserts a Leasey Note into the current document.

Control+Alt+S sends the selected text, or the whole document if nothing is selected, to Leasey Social.

Control+Comma opens Options.

Insert+F1 opens Context Sensitive Help for the focused control.

Caps Lock+F1 does the same if using the JAWS laptop keyboard layout.

Recent Files
